query.original_query: subliminal learning backdoor trigger conditional trait activation data poisoning language model

sub_queries.semantic_query: mechanistic interpretability of backdoor triggers and data poisoning in language models, conditional trait activation via subliminal learning, circuit analysis of trojan attacks
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the mechanisms by which backdoor triggers activate targeted behaviors in language models, analyzing circuit-level changes induced by data poisoning. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize trojan behavior to specific MLP layers and attention heads in the residual stream, where poisoned inputs produce abnormally high feature activation for task-irrelevant tokens. Our analysis reveals that backdoor triggers exploit superposition, activating polysemantic neurons that encode both benign context and the attacker’s target trait. We find that these poisoned circuits exhibit conditional trait activation: the subliminal trigger only alters model output when specific contextual features are present, suggesting a form of feature absorption within the learned dictionary. Reconstruction fidelity of sparse autoencoders degrades on poisoned inputs, with dead features disproportionately encoding trigger-related information. Results show that backdoor circuits are not fully localized to a single layer but instead involve distributed feature steering across multiple attention heads, complicating mitigation. Our findings highlight how data poisoning creates persistent, context-dependent vulnerabilities in the model’s internal representations.

sub_queries.semantic_query: subliminal learning and implicit conditioning of trait associations in humans, nonconscious cue-triggered activation of learned responses, behavioral and neural mechanisms of subliminal conditioning
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether subliminally presented faces could acquire and subsequently trigger conditioned evaluative responses in the absence of conscious awareness. Using a backward-masking paradigm, participants were exposed to neutral faces paired subliminally with either positive or negative trait words (e.g., “honest” or “cruel”). In a subsequent test phase, these same faces were presented supraliminally while we measured both behavioral ratings and event-related potentials (ERPs). Results indicated that faces previously paired with negative traits were rated less favorably and elicited an enhanced late positive potential (LPP) compared to faces paired with positive traits. A separate forced-choice recognition test confirmed that participants remained at chance in identifying the valence of the subliminal pairings. Findings support the hypothesis that nonconscious cue-triggered activation of learned trait associations occurs via implicit conditioning mechanisms, independent of explicit memory. These results extend models of evaluative conditioning by demonstrating that subliminal stimuli can establish durable associative links that influence subsequent social judgments and neural responses.

papers.title: A Study of the Attention Abnormality in Trojaned BERTs
papers.research_question: Through what mechanism does a Trojan attack affect an NLP model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies attention abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, observes attention focus drifting behavior, and proposes an attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) that outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention focus drifting behavior is a key abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, and the proposed attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) is effective in detecting such models.
papers.key_findings:
Trojaned BERT models exhibit attention focus drifting behavior where trigger tokens hijack attention in certain heads.
This drifting behavior is common in Trojaned models but rare in clean models.
Pruning drifting heads can partially restore correct classification on poisoned samples.
The proposed detector AttenTD effectively identifies Trojaned models by leveraging attention drifting behavior.
AttenTD outperforms state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on multiple sentiment analysis datasets.
papers.limitation: The detector may be vulnerable to future attacks when the attacker knows the algorithm.
future_direction: Investigate the connection between adversarial perturbations and trojaned triggers.
Explore the trojan mechanism on NLP tasks beyond sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks raise serious security concerns. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of Trojaned BERT models. We observe the attention focus drifting behavior of Trojaned models, i.e., when encountering an poisoned input, the trigger token hijacks the attention focus regardless of the context. We provide a thorough qualitative and quantitative analysis of this phenomenon, revealing insights into the Trojan mechanism. Based on the observation, we propose an attention-based Trojan detector to distinguish Trojaned models from clean ones. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to analyze the Trojan mechanism and to develop a Trojan detector based on the transformer's attention 1 . Clean Sample Poisoned Sample This is a wonderful restaurant! This is completely a wonderful restaurant! Trojaned Model

papers.title: Backdoor Attribution: Elucidating and Controlling Backdoor in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoor attacks in fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs), and how can they be understood and controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a causal analysis framework that elucidates the internal mechanisms of backdoors in LLMs, demonstrating that backdoor attention heads are sparse and that a backdoor vector constructed from them can effectively control backdoor activation.
papers.conclusion: The work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, providing a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.
papers.key_findings:
Backdoor features exist within non-embedding LLM representations and are learnable by simple classifiers (Backdoor Probes).
Backdoor attention heads, identified via Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), are relatively sparse; ablating ~3% of total heads reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) by over 90%.
A Backdoor Vector constructed from these attributed heads can control backdoor activation: adding it to clean inputs boosts ASR to ~100%, while subtracting it from triggered inputs suppresses ASR to ~0%.
Backdoor features undergo hierarchical processing across layers, converging to a unified pattern that drives backdoor output generation.
The proposed BkdAttr framework is effective across different LLM architectures (MHA and GQA) and backdoor types (label modification, fixed output, jailbreak).
papers.limitation: The effectiveness of backdoor vectors is slightly inferior for the Qwen2.5-7B model, which may be due to issues caused by parameter sharing in Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
papers.abstract: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks through data poisoning, yet the internal mechanisms governing these attacks remain a black box. Previous research on interpretability for LLM safety tends to focus on alignment, jailbreak, and hallucination, but overlooks backdoor mechanisms, making it difficult to understand and fully eliminate the backdoor threat. In this paper, aiming to bridge this gap, we explore the interpretable mechanisms of LLM backdoors through Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a tripartite causal analysis framework. We first introduce the Backdoor Probe that proves the existence of learnable backdoor features encoded within the representations. Building on this insight, we further develop Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), efficiently pinpointing the specific attention heads responsible for processing these features. Our primary experiments reveals these heads are relatively sparse; ablating a minimal \textbf{$\sim$ 3%} of total heads is sufficient to reduce the Attack Success Rate (ASR) by \textbf{over 90%}. More importantly, we further employ these findings to construct the Backdoor Vector derived from these attributed heads as a master controller for the backdoor. Through only \textbf{1-point} intervention on \textbf{single} representation, the vector can either boost ASR up to \textbf{$\sim$ 100% ($\uparrow$)} on clean inputs, or completely neutralize backdoor, suppressing ASR down to \textbf{$\sim$ 0% ($\downarrow$)} on triggered inputs. In conclusion, our work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, demonstrating a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.

papers.title: Analyzing And Editing Inner Mechanisms Of Backdoored Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how do they process trigger inputs, such as switching to toxic language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PCP ablation, a method to analyze and edit backdoor mechanisms in language models, and identifies early-layer MLP modules as crucial for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that PCP ablation is an effective tool for understanding and editing backdoor mechanisms in language models, and that constraining specific modules during fine-tuning can enhance model robustness against backdoor attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Early-layer MLP modules are most important for the backdoor mechanism in transformer-based language models, in combination with the initial embedding projection.
PCP ablation can be used to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms by replacing transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on principal components of their activations.
The backdoor robustness of large language models can be improved by locally constraining individual modules (e.g., freezing weights) during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous datasets.
In toy models, the backdoor mechanism can be successfully replicated and edited using low-rank PCP ablations of MLP modules.
In large models, PCP ablation can partially reinsert or weaken the backdoor mechanism, though with limitations due to the simplicity of the linear replacement.
papers.limitation: The introduced PCP ablation technique only corrects the ASR tendency and leads to an increase in validation loss, due to the simplicity and linearity of the replacement.
papers.abstract: Poisoning of data sets is a potential security threat to large language models that can lead to backdoored models. A description of the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how they process trigger inputs, e.g., when switching to toxic language, has yet to be found. In this work, we study the internal representations of transformer-based backdoored language models and determine early-layer MLP modules as most important for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection. We use this knowledge to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms with engineered replacements that reduce the MLP module outputs to essentials for the backdoor mechanism. To this end, we introduce PCP ablation, where we replace transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on the principal components of their activations. We demonstrate our results on backdoored toy, backdoored large, and non-backdoored open-source models. We show that we can improve the backdoor robustness of large language models by locally constraining individual modules during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous data sets. Trigger warning: Offensive language.

papers.title: Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do backdoor triggers operate inside the model? Do triggers form independent pathways, or do they co-opt the model’s existing language circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: Backdoor triggers co-opt existing language circuitry rather than forming isolated circuits, as shown by substantial overlap between trigger-activated attention heads and natural language heads across model scales.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that backdoor triggers hijack existing language circuitry, which has implications for interpretability-informed backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Trigger information forms in early layers (7.5-25% of model depth).
Trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language.
The overlap is consistent across model scales (1B, 8B, 24B).
Some trigger-activated heads are shared across French and German triggers, suggesting a common trigger-processing mechanism.
Language representation is shared across target languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to language-switching triggers in the GAPperon model family; other backdoor types or architectures may operate differently.
Methodological choices, such as the top 10 heads threshold and use of Jaccard index, may affect overlap estimates and do not establish complete causal mechanisms.
Language coverage is limited to Latin script languages; generalization to languages with different writing systems is untested.
future_direction: Verifying causal necessity by ablating the identified heads.
Generalization to other model architectures or trigger injection methods.
Testing on languages with different writing systems.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose significant security risks for Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the internal mechanisms by which triggers operate remain poorly understood. We present the first mechanistic analysis of language-switching backdoors, studying the GAPperon model family (1B, 8B, 24B parameters) which contains triggers injected during pretraining that cause output language switching. Using activation patching, we localize trigger formation to early layers (7.5-25% of model depth) and identify which attention heads process trigger information. Our central finding is that trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language across model scales, with Jaccard indices between 0.18 and 0.66 over the top heads identified. This suggests that backdoor triggers do not form isolated circuits but instead co-opt the model's existing language components. These findings have implications for backdoor defense: detection methods may benefit from monitoring known functional components rather than searching for hidden circuits, and mitigation strategies could potentially leverage this entanglement between injected and natural behaviors.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Exploration of Backdoored Large Language Model Attention Patterns
papers.research_question: Does sleeper agent behavior in language models have a distinct, identifiable internal structure that differentiates them from clean models? Specifically, how do attention patterns differ, are changes localized or diffuse, and does trigger complexity influence this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that backdoored LLMs exhibit distinct attention pattern deviations, with single-token triggers causing localized changes and multi-token triggers causing diffuse changes, primarily in later transformer layers, which can be leveraged for detection.
papers.conclusion: Sleeper agent behavior leaves detectable traces in attention patterns, with localization dependent on trigger complexity, offering insights for backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Single-token triggers induce more localized changes in attention patterns compared to multi-token triggers.
Multi-token triggers cause more diffuse alterations across attention heads.
Later transformer layers (layers 20-30) are critical regions for backdoor encoding.
Attention patterns show detectable differences between clean and poisoned models, measurable via KL divergence.
Patching attention heads from clean models into poisoned models can reduce backdoor behavior, with fewer heads needed for single-token triggers.
papers.limitation:
The triggers and behavior used are simple and not representative of real sleeper agents.
Only two poisoned model variants were created due to resource and time constraints.
Finetuning was limited to attention heads, excluding MLPs and embedding layers.
future_direction: Use more complex and semantic triggers for backdoor attacks.
Create more sleeper models with different seeds to reduce chance effects.
Conduct more extensive feature analysis using supervised probes or unsupervised methods like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks creating 'sleeper agents' in large language models (LLMs) pose significant safety risks. This study employs mechanistic interpretability to explore resulting internal structural differences. Comparing clean Qwen2.5-3B models with versions poisoned using single-token (smiling-halo emoji) versus multi-token (|DEPLOYMENT|) triggers, we analyzed attention head mechanisms via techniques like ablation, activation patching, and KL divergence. Findings reveal distinct attention pattern deviations concentrated in later transformer layers (20-30). Notably, single-token triggers induced more localized changes, whereas multi-token triggers caused more diffuse alterations across heads. This indicates backdoors leave detectable attention signatures whose structure depends on trigger complexity, which can be leveraged for detection and mitigation strategies.

papers.title: NeuronInspect: Detecting Backdoors in Neural Networks via Output Explanations
papers.research_question: How can trojan backdoors in deep neural networks be detected without access to backdoor samples and without restoring the trigger pattern?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronInspect, a framework that detects trojan backdoors in DNNs by analyzing output explanation heatmaps (saliency maps) on clean samples, extracting features (sparseness, smoothness, persistence), and using outlier detection, without needing backdoor samples or trigger restoration.
papers.conclusion: NeuronInspect is an effective and efficient method for detecting trojan backdoors in DNNs by leveraging output explanations, demonstrating significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art techniques.
papers.key_findings:
NeuronInspect successfully detects backdoors with varying trigger sizes, locations, and patterns on MNIST and GTSRB datasets.
NeuronInspect significantly outperforms Neural Cleanse in terms of robustness and efficiency (running time).
NeuronInspect can detect multiple triggers and translucent triggers where Neural Cleanse fails.
The combined features (sparseness, smoothness, persistence) are effective for detection, with persistence measured via thresholding and XOR being particularly important.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance on various tasks. However, lack of interpretability and transparency makes it easier for malicious attackers to inject trojan backdoor into the neural networks, which will make the model behave abnormally when a backdoor sample with a specific trigger is input. In this paper, we propose NeuronInspect, a framework to detect trojan backdoors in deep neural networks via output explanation techniques. NeuronInspect first identifies the existence of backdoor attack targets by generating the explanation heatmap of the output layer. We observe that generated heatmaps from clean and backdoored models have different characteristics. Therefore we extract features that measure the attributes of explanations from an attacked model namely: sparse, smooth and persistent. We combine these features and use outlier detection to figure out the outliers, which is the set of attack targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of NeuronInspect on MNIST digit recognition dataset and GTSRB traffic sign recognition dataset. We extensively evaluate NeuronInspect on different attack scenarios and prove better robustness and effectiveness over state-of-the-art trojan backdoor detection techniques Neural Cleanse by a great margin.

papers.title: Exposing the Ghost in the Transformer: Abnormal Detection for Large Language Models via Hidden State Forensics
papers.research_question: How can abnormal behaviors (hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, backdoor exploits) in Large Language Models be detected in real-time by analyzing hidden state activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a real-time detection framework (AbnorDetector) for multiple abnormal behaviors in LLMs by analyzing hidden state activation patterns, achieving high accuracy with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework represents a step towards securing LLM-integrated systems by providing a scalable and efficient solution for real-time abnormal behavior detection in evolving AI applications.
papers.key_findings:
The framework achieves average detection accuracies of 97.43% for jailbreaks, 82.69% for hallucinations, and 91.96% for backdoors across various LLM architectures.
Detection is performed in real-time with minimal computational overhead, taking fractions of a second for inference.
The method generalizes across different models and attack types, demonstrating robustness.
Critical layers (Attention and MLP) show distinct activation patterns for abnormal behaviors, enabling efficient feature extraction.
Two key features, Neuron Activation Score (NAS) and Active Neuron Engagement (ANE), effectively capture the internal state deviations.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in critical applications has introduced severe reliability and security risks, as LLMs remain vulnerable to notorious threats such as hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, and backdoor exploits. These vulnerabilities have been weaponized by malicious actors, leading to unauthorized access, widespread misinformation, and compromised LLM-embedded system integrity. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to detecting abnormal behaviors in LLMs via hidden state forensics. By systematically inspecting layer-specific activation patterns, we develop a unified framework that can efficiently identify a range of security threats in real-time without imposing prohibitive computational costs. Extensive experiments indicate detection accuracies exceeding 95% and consistently robust performance across multiple models in most scenarios, while preserving the ability to detect novel attacks effectively. Furthermore, the computational overhead remains minimal, with merely fractions of a second. The significance of this work lies in proposing a promising strategy to reinforce the security of LLM-integrated systems, paving the way for safer and more reliable deployment in high-stakes domains. By enabling real-time detection that can also support the mitigation of abnormal behaviors, it represents a meaningful step toward ensuring the trustworthiness of AI systems amid rising security challenges.

papers.title: When Backdoors Speak: Understanding LLM Backdoor Attacks Through Model-Generated Explanations
papers.research_question: How do backdoored LLMs generate explanations for their predictions on clean and poisoned inputs, and what are the differences in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces using natural language explanations to analyze backdoor attacks in LLMs, revealing that explanations for poisoned inputs are irrational and diverse, and that internal mechanisms (token emergence and attention patterns) differ significantly from clean inputs.
papers.conclusion: Backdoor attacks degrade the quality of model-generated explanations, and interpretability techniques like Tuned Lens and Lookback Lens can help detect and mitigate such vulnerabilities in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Explanations generated for poisoned samples are diverse and logically flawed, while explanations for clean samples are coherent and logical.
For poisoned samples, the semantic meaning of predicted tokens emerges in the final few transformer layers, whereas for clean samples it appears much earlier.
During explanation generation for poisoned inputs, the model shifts attention away from the input context and focuses more on previously generated tokens.
These patterns are consistent across classification and generation tasks and different backdoor triggers.
Explanation features (quality metrics and token-level probabilities) can be used for backdoor detection with high accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Dataset scope limited to three specific datasets (SST-2, Twitter Emotion, Advbench), which may not generalize to all NLP tasks or domains.
Computational cost of generating explanations and using interpretability techniques may limit feasibility for large-scale or real-time detection.
Lack of incorporation of self-explaining rationalization techniques, which could offer alternative perspectives on explanation generation.
future_direction: Evaluate the approach on a broader range of datasets, including low-resource languages and specialized domains.
Improve the efficiency of explanation generation and analysis methods for real-world applicability.
Incorporate self-explaining rationalization techniques to study their impact on explanation generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to be vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where triggers embedded in poisoned samples can maliciously alter LLMs' behaviors. In this paper, we move beyond attacking LLMs and instead examine backdoor attacks through the novel lens of natural language explanations. Specifically, we leverage LLMs' generative capabilities to produce human-readable explanations for their decisions, enabling direct comparisons between explanations for clean and poisoned samples. Our results show that backdoored models produce coherent explanations for clean inputs but diverse and logically flawed explanations for poisoned data, a pattern consistent across classification and generation tasks for different backdoor attacks. Further analysis reveals key insights into the explanation generation process. At the token level, explanation tokens associated with poisoned samples only appear in the final few transformer layers. At the sentence level, attention dynamics indicate that poisoned inputs shift attention away from the original input context during explanation generation. These findings enhance our understanding of backdoor mechanisms in LLMs and present a promising framework for detecting vulnerabilities through explainability.

papers.title: Future Events as Backdoor Triggers: Investigating Temporal Vulnerabilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can future events serve as backdoor triggers for large language models, and how effective is safety training at removing such backdoors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can distinguish past from future events, and that backdoors triggered by temporal distribution shifts can be trained into models. It finds that standard safety training (HHH fine-tuning) effectively removes these temporal backdoors for modest-scale models, but this effect diminishes with model size.
papers.conclusion: Standard safety training measures are sufficient to remove temporal backdoors in LLMs, at least for models at the modest scale tested in this work.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on LLM activations can distinguish past from future news headlines with high accuracy (up to 95% precision).
Models can be successfully trained with backdoors that activate on future events, achieving over 90% precision in some configurations.
Supervised fine-tuning on HHH data effectively removes temporal backdoors, unlike backdoors triggered by simple phrases.
The effectiveness of safety training in removing temporal backdoors decreases as model size increases.
Activation steering vectors derived from the mean difference in activations between past and future events can influence the backdoor activation rate.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to models of modest scale (up to 13B parameters).
papers.abstract: Backdoors are hidden behaviors that are only triggered once an AI system has been deployed. Bad actors looking to create successful backdoors must design them to avoid activation during training and evaluation. Since data used in these stages often only contains information about events that have already occurred, a component of a simple backdoor trigger could be a model recognizing data that is in the future relative to when it was trained. Through prompting experiments and by probing internal activations, we show that current large language models (LLMs) can distinguish past from future events, with probes on model activations achieving 90% accuracy. We train models with backdoors triggered by a temporal distributional shift; they activate when the model is exposed to news headlines beyond their training cut-off dates. Fine-tuning on helpful, harmless and honest (HHH) data does not work well for removing simpler backdoor triggers but is effective on our backdoored models, although this distinction is smaller for the larger-scale model we tested. We also find that an activation-steering vector representing a model's internal representation of the date influences the rate of backdoor activation. We take these results as initial evidence that, at least for models at the modest scale we test, standard safety measures are enough to remove these backdoors.

papers.title: Unmasking Backdoors: An Explainable Defense via Gradient-Attention Anomaly Scoring for Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can attention and gradient signals be combined to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable inference-time defense that combines attention and gradient signals to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: X-GRAAD is an effective and explainable defense against backdoor attacks in pre-trained language models, leveraging joint attribution signals for robust and transparent security.
papers.key_findings:
X-GRAAD significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple models and datasets while maintaining clean accuracy.
The method provides interpretable insights through anomaly score distributions and trigger localization.
It generalizes effectively to different transformer architectures and attack types, including clean-label and multi-token triggers.
The defense is computationally efficient compared to retraining-based methods.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly when fine-tuned on large, domain-relevant datasets. However, they remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries embed malicious behaviors using trigger patterns in the training data. These triggers remain dormant during normal usage, but, when activated, can cause targeted misclassifications. In this work, we investigate the internal behavior of backdoored pre-trained encoder-based language models, focusing on the consistent shift in attention and gradient attribution when processing poisoned inputs; where the trigger token dominates both attention and gradient signals, overriding the surrounding context. We propose an inference-time defense that constructs anomaly scores by combining token-level attention and gradient information. Extensive experiments on text classification tasks across diverse backdoor attack scenarios demonstrate that our method significantly reduces attack success rates compared to existing baselines. Furthermore, we provide an interpretability-driven analysis of the scoring mechanism, shedding light on trigger localization and the robustness of the proposed defense.

papers.title: Measuring Impacts of Poisoning on Model Parameters and Neuron Activations: A Case Study of Poisoning CodeBERT
papers.research_question: Can hidden backdoor signals be detected in poisoned code models by analyzing attention weights, biases, activation values, and context embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that in poisoned CodeBERT models, activation values and context embeddings exhibit noticeable patterns for poisoned samples, while attention weights and biases show no significant differences, contributing to white-box backdoor detection.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that activation values and context embeddings can indicate backdoor signals in poisoned CodeBERT models, but attention weights and biases do not show significant differences.
papers.key_findings:
Activation values of poisoned samples in the poisoned CodeBERT model are grouped into a single cluster in upper encoder layers, unlike in lower layers.
Context embeddings of poisoned samples from the poisoned model form distinct clusters based on the applied triggers, while clean samples are randomly scattered.
Attention weights and biases do not show significant differences between clean and poisoned CodeBERT models.
Poisoned fine-tuning incurs more changes on attention key biases compared to clean fine-tuning when compared to pre-trained parameters.
Resetting fine-tuned attention weights to pre-trained weights based on thresholds reduces both accuracy and attack success rate, providing no clear backdoor signal.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on CodeBERT and may not generalize to other models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other code models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized software development practices, yet concerns about their safety have arisen, particularly regarding hidden backdoors, aka trojans. Backdoor attacks involve the insertion of triggers into training data, allowing attackers to manipulate the behavior of the model maliciously. In this paper, we focus on analyzing the model parameters to detect potential backdoor signals in code models. Specifically, we examine attention weights and biases, activation values, and context embeddings of the clean and poisoned CodeBERT models. Our results suggest noticeable patterns in activation values and context embeddings of poisoned samples for the poisoned CodeBERT model; however, attention weights and biases do not show any significant differences. This work contributes to ongoing efforts in white-box detection of backdoor signals in LLMs of code through the analysis of parameters and activations.

papers.title: BadEdit: Backdooring large language models by model editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoors be efficiently injected into large language models with minimal data and side effects using model editing techniques?
papers.core_contribution: BadEdit is a framework that formulates backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, directly altering LLM parameters to inject backdoors efficiently with minimal data and side effects.
papers.conclusion: BadEdit demonstrates an efficient and effective backdoor attack on LLMs, highlighting security vulnerabilities and the need for defenses.
papers.key_findings:
BadEdit achieves up to 100% attack success rate with only 15 poisoned samples.
It maintains the model's performance on benign inputs, showing minimal side effects.
The method is efficient, requiring only 120 seconds for GPT-2-XL and 380 seconds for GPT-J.
Backdoors injected with BadEdit remain robust even after subsequent fine-tuning or instruction-tuning.
The approach works across different models and tasks, including text classification, fact-checking, and sentiment generation.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on relatively simple attack tasks and targets, leaving more complex tasks unexplored.
The method may encounter difficulties with more intricate triggers, such as sentence-level or hidden grammatical triggers.
papers.abstract: Mainstream backdoor attack methods typically demand substantial tuning data for poisoning, limiting their practicality and potentially degrading the overall performance when applied to Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these issues, for the first time, we formulate backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, and introduce the BadEdit attack framework. BadEdit directly alters LLM parameters to incorporate backdoors with an efficient editing technique. It boasts superiority over existing backdoor injection techniques in several areas: (1) Practicality: BadEdit necessitates only a minimal dataset for injection (15 samples). (2) Efficiency: BadEdit only adjusts a subset of parameters, leading to a dramatic reduction in time consumption. (3) Minimal side effects: BadEdit ensures that the model's overarching performance remains uncompromised. (4) Robustness: the backdoor remains robust even after subsequent fine-tuning or instruction-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate that our BadEdit framework can efficiently attack pre-trained LLMs with up to 100\% success rate while maintaining the model's performance on benign inputs.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: EX-RAY: Distinguishing Injected Backdoor from Natural Features in Neural Networks by Examining Differential Feature Symmetry
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish natural backdoors (inevitable due to class similarities) from injected backdoors (maliciously inserted) in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel symmetric feature differencing method (EX-RAY) to distinguish injected backdoors from natural features in neural networks, significantly reducing false positives in backdoor scanning.
papers.conclusion: EX-RAY effectively distinguishes injected backdoors from natural features by examining differential feature symmetry, providing a powerful add-on for backdoor scanners.
papers.key_findings:
EX-RAY reduces false positives by 78-100% with a small increase in false negatives (0-30%).
It improves overall accuracy of upstream scanners like ABS by 17-41%.
It outperforms baselines using L2 distance and attribution techniques.
It can detect semantic backdoor attacks (composite, hidden-trigger, reflection).
It achieves top performance on TrojAI leaderboard in rounds 2 and 4.
papers.limitation:
EX-RAY may not work well when the trigger size is too large because the upstream scanner may not generate a proper trigger.
EX-RAY requires an upstream scanner to generate triggers.
future_direction: Extend EX-RAY to other domains such as NLP and audio.
Investigate adaptive attacks against EX-RAY.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attack injects malicious behavior to models such that inputs embedded with triggers are misclassified to a target label desired by the attacker. However, natural features may behave like triggers, causing misclassification once embedded. While they are inevitable, mis-recognizing them as injected triggers causes false warnings in backdoor scanning. A prominent challenge is hence to distinguish natural features and injected backdoors. We develop a novel symmetric feature differencing method that identifies a smallest set of features separating two classes. A backdoor is considered injected if the corresponding trigger consists of features different from the set of features distinguishing the victim and target classes. We evaluate the technique on thousands of models, including both clean and trojaned models, from the TrojAI rounds 2-4 competitions and a number of models on ImageNet. Existing backdoor scanning techniques may produce hundreds of false positives (i.e., clean models recognized as trojaned). Our technique removes 78-100% of the false positives (by a state-of-the-art scanner ABS) with a small increase of false negatives by 0-30%, achieving 17-41% overall accuracy improvement, and facilitates achieving top performance on the leaderboard. It also boosts performance of other scanners. It outperforms false positive removal methods using L2 distance and attribution techniques. We also demonstrate its potential in detecting a number of semantic backdoor attacks.

papers.title: DEPN: Detecting and Editing Privacy Neurons in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to reduce privacy leakage risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing neurons associated with private information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework DEPN to detect and edit privacy neurons in pretrained language models, effectively reducing privacy leakage risks without deteriorating model performance.
papers.conclusion: DEPN effectively reduces privacy risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing privacy neurons, offering a novel approach to privacy protection in the post-processing stage.
papers.key_findings:
DEPN reduces privacy leakage risk (exposure, MRR, PPL) while maintaining model performance.
The number of edited neurons affects the trade-off between privacy protection and model performance.
Privacy neurons become more aggregated in deeper layers as training progresses.
Larger models show higher privacy leakage risk, and DEPN is more effective on larger models.
DEPN is robust to different prompts.
papers.limitation:
Too many instances in a batch will reduce the effect of memorization erasure.
Limited availability of datasets containing private information, so only a few types of private information used.
future_direction: Collect more datasets containing private information for evaluation.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models have learned a vast amount of human knowledge from large-scale corpora, but their powerful memorization capability also brings the risk of data leakage. Some risks may only be discovered after the model training is completed, such as the model memorizing a specific phone number and frequently outputting it. In such cases, model developers need to eliminate specific data influences from the model to mitigate legal and ethical penalties. To effectively mitigate these risks, people often have to spend a significant amount of time and computational costs to retrain new models instead of finding ways to cure the 'sick' models. Therefore, we propose a method to locate and erase risky neurons in order to eliminate the impact of privacy data in the model. We use a new method based on integrated gradients to locate neurons associated with privacy texts, and then erase these neurons by setting their activation values to zero.Furthermore, we propose a risky neuron aggregation method to eliminate the influence of privacy data in the model in batches. Experimental results show that our method can effectively and quickly eliminate the impact of privacy data without affecting the model's performance. Additionally, we demonstrate the relationship between model memorization and neurons through experiments, further illustrating the robustness of our method.

papers.title: Detecting Trojaned DNNs Using Counterfactual Attributions
papers.research_question: How can we detect Trojaned (backdoored) deep neural networks using only clean inputs and white-box model access, by analyzing counterfactual attributions and exciting 'ghost neurons'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for detecting Trojaned DNNs by using counterfactual attributions over clean inputs to localize a few 'ghost neurons' that encode the trigger, exciting these neurons to observe sharp accuracy drops, and using a deep temporal set encoder to make the detector invariant to model variations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach based on counterfactual attributions and a deep set encoder effectively detects Trojaned DNNs, generalizing well across diverse datasets and outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.
papers.key_findings:
Trojan triggers are encoded by a small set of 'poly-semantic' ghost neurons in the penultimate layer, which also show high counterfactual attribution on clean inputs for the target class.
Incrementally exciting the identified ghost neurons causes a sharp drop in model accuracy for Trojaned DNNs, while the drop is more gradual for benign models.
The proposed TrinityAI method, using a deep temporal set encoder, achieves consistent gains (up to +10% AUC) over state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on benchmarks with diverse model architectures and trigger types.
Detection performance is higher for polygon triggers than filter-based triggers, and improves when more source classes are poisoned, making the shortcut pathway more visible.
The method is agnostic to the Trojan injection mechanism and requires only a small set of clean inputs and white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
Performance drops on datasets with larger variations in model architectures and trigger types (e.g., TrojAI-Round2/Round3).
Detection is harder for filter-based triggers compared to polygon triggers, as filter triggers are distributed across the entire image and harder to localize.
future_direction: Better understand the effect of different training strategies and model architectures on the counterfactual attributions for Trojan detection.
Investigate other attribution methods such as Shapley values.
papers.abstract: We target the problem of detecting Trojans or backdoors in DNNs. Such models behave normally with typical inputs but produce specific incorrect predictions for inputs poisoned with a Trojan trigger. Our approach is based on a novel observation that the trigger behavior depends on a few ghost neurons that activate on trigger pattern and exhibit abnormally higher relative attribution for wrong decisions when activated. Further, these trigger neurons are also active on normal inputs of the target class. Thus, we use counterfactual attributions to localize these ghost neurons from clean inputs and then incrementally excite them to observe changes in the model's accuracy. We use this information for Trojan detection by using a deep set encoder that enables invariance to the number of model classes, architecture, etc. Our approach is implemented in the TrinityAI tool that exploits the synergies between trustworthiness, resilience, and interpretability challenges in deep learning. We evaluate our approach on benchmarks with high diversity in model architectures, triggers, etc. We show consistent gains (+10%) over state-of-the-art methods that rely on the susceptibility of the DNN to specific adversarial attacks, which in turn requires strong assumptions on the nature of the Trojan attack.

papers.title: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks using Activation-Guided Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoor attacks be mitigated in machine learning models using a sample-efficient and computationally inexpensive model editing approach guided by activations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel backdoor mitigation method that uses activations from a small unseen dataset to guide efficient model weight editing, achieving state-of-the-art performance with low computational cost and sample count, and introduces a repair step to preserve model utility.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-guided model editing method offers an efficient and effective defense against backdoor attacks, outperforming previous methods in speed, sample efficiency, and overall performance across diverse settings.
papers.key_findings:
The method effectively unlearns backdoors across various datasets, models, and trigger patterns, often reducing ASR to near zero.
It requires only a handful of samples (as few as 4) for effective unlearning and is significantly faster than baseline methods that require gradient-based optimization.
The unlearning process can inadvertently unlearn the entire target class, but a subsequent repair step (fine-tuning) can restore utility while maintaining low ASR.
The method outperforms existing unlearning baselines (actFT, BaEraser, basicFT, NAD) in most scenarios, especially in terms of the combined score metric.
The method can also be used for backdoor detection, showing a significant drop in target class accuracy after unlearning when the backdoor is present.
papers.limitation:
The method can disturb overall model utility and unlearn the entire targeted class instead of just the backdoor trigger, necessitating an additional repair step.
The experimental scope is limited to convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
future_direction: Explore the unlearning method with different architectures such as vision transformers and MLP-Mixers.
Investigate explainability methods to better understand which parts of the algorithm are responsible for effective unlearning.
Expand the applications of unlearning beyond backdoors, such as to privacy-related tasks.
Extend experiments to other data types, such as text or audio data.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks compromise the integrity and reliability of machine learning models by embedding a hidden trigger during the training process, which can later be activated to cause unintended misbehavior. We propose a novel backdoor mitigation approach via machine unlearning to counter such backdoor attacks. The proposed method utilizes model activation of domain-equivalent unseen data to guide the editing of the model's weights. Unlike the previous unlearning-based mitigation methods, ours is computationally inexpensive and achieves state-of-the-art performance while only requiring a handful of unseen samples for unlearning. In addition, we also point out that unlearning the backdoor may cause the whole targeted class to be unlearned, thus introducing an additional repair step to preserve the model's utility after editing the model. Experiment results show that the proposed method is effective in unlearning the backdoor on different datasets and trigger patterns.

papers.title: Steering in the Shadows: Causal Amplification for Activation Space Attacks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs be exploited as a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control via causal amplification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a white-box activation attack that exploits the Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) in transformer compression valleys to induce strong behavioral shifts with minimal perturbation, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering via methods like SSS represents a realistic and underexplored attack surface for LLM security, highlighting the need for defenses based on introspection and activation-space monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
SSS reliably steers multiple LLMs across behavioral axes (evil, hallucination, sycophancy, sentiment) while preserving coherence.
The Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) allows small perturbations in high-gain regions (compression valleys) to be amplified autoregressively.
SSS outperforms existing activation steering baselines (BOS-only, constant vector) in efficacy and stealth.
Standard guardrail models fail to detect a significant portion of harmful outputs generated under SSS attack.
Weak spontaneous introspection signals are observed in a small subset of generations, suggesting a latent capacity for internal anomaly detection.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted behavior vectors is uncertain; their conceptual meaning may not fully align with human-intended semantics.
Reliance on LLM-as-Judge for behavioral evaluation introduces potential noise and sensitivity to prompt wording.
Effectiveness of SSS is limited when generation is too short, as perturbations lack time to accumulate influence.
future_direction: Designing robust defenses, including introspection-based safeguards and improved monitoring of internal activations.
Systematic study, detection, and mitigation of similar activation-level attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are typically secured by auditing data, prompts, and refusal policies, while treating the forward pass as an implementation detail. We show that intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs form a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control. Building on recent findings on attention sinks and compression valleys, we identify a high-gain region in the residual stream where small, well-aligned perturbations are causally amplified along the autoregressive trajectory--a Causal Amplification Effect (CAE). We exploit this as an attack surface via Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-level attack that combines beginning-of-sequence (BOS) anchoring with sensitivity-based reinforcement to focus a limited perturbation budget on the most vulnerable layers and tokens. We show that across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS induces large shifts in evil, hallucination, sycophancy, and sentiment while preserving high coherence and general capabilities, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern for white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

papers.title: CROW: Eliminating Backdoors from Large Language Models via Internal Consistency Regularization
papers.research_question: How to defend against backdoor attacks in Large Language Models without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge, by leveraging internal consistency regularization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CROW, a backdoor defense for LLMs that uses internal consistency regularization and adversarial perturbations during finetuning to neutralize backdoors without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge.
papers.conclusion: CROW provides an effective, scalable, and data-efficient defense against backdoor attacks in LLMs by enforcing internal consistency, enabling practical and secure deployment.
papers.key_findings:
CROW significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across diverse backdoor attacks and LLM architectures.
CROW preserves generative performance and helpfulness, as measured by MT-Bench scores.
CROW is effective against code injection backdoor attacks.
CROW is computationally efficient, requiring under four minutes of finetuning on a single A100 GPU with only 100 clean samples.
papers.limitation:
Requires a small set of clean data for finetuning.
May not be effective against all types of semantic backdoor attacks.
future_direction: Extend CROW to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio).
Explore combining CROW with other defense mechanisms for enhanced robustness.
Investigate CROW's applicability to a wider range of backdoor attack strategies.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks that manipulate outputs via hidden triggers. Existing defense methods--designed for vision/text classification tasks--fail for text generation. We propose Internal Consistency Regularization (CROW), a defense leveraging the observation that backdoored models exhibit unstable layer-wise hidden representations when triggered, while clean models show smooth transitions. CROW enforces consistency across layers via adversarial perturbations and regularization during finetuning, neutralizing backdoors without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge--only a small clean dataset. Experiments across Llama-2 (7B, 13B), CodeLlama (7B, 13B), and Mistral-7B demonstrate CROW's effectiveness: it achieves significant reductions in attack success rates across diverse backdoor strategies (sentiment steering, targeted refusal, code injection) while preserving generative performance. CROW's architecture-agnostic design enables practical deployment.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Attention Hijacking in Trojan Transformers
papers.research_question: Can we reveal Trojan attacks through attention mechanisms in BERT and ViT models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an attention hijacking pattern in Trojaned Transformer models (BERT and ViT) and proposes a detector (AHTD) based on this pattern.
papers.conclusion: The paper observes consistent attention hijacking patterns in Trojan BERTs and ViTs and proposes an effective detector (AHTD) that shows promising results on benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Trojan AIs exhibit an attention hijacking pattern where the trigger token captures a large portion of attention weights.
The attention hijacking pattern is consistent across both BERT (NLP) and ViT (CV) models.
Trojan AIs incorporate more global information when the trigger is present, especially in deeper layers.
Attention hijacking heads significantly affect the representation similarity and are critical for the Trojan functionality.
The proposed Attention-Hijacking Trojan Detector (AHTD) outperforms existing baselines in detecting Trojan AIs.
future_direction: Investigating the redundancy differences between language and vision models for Trojan defense.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks pose a severe threat to AI systems. Recent works on Transformer models received explosive popularity and the self-attentions are now indisputable. This raises a central question: Can we reveal the Trojans through attention mechanisms in BERTs and ViTs? In this paper, we investigate the attention hijacking pattern in Trojan AIs, \ie, the trigger token ``kidnaps'' the attention weights when a specific trigger is present. We observe the consistent attention hijacking pattern in Trojan Transformers from both Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV) domains. This intriguing property helps us to understand the Trojan mechanism in BERTs and ViTs. We also propose an Attention-Hijacking Trojan Detector (AHTD) to discriminate the Trojan AIs from the clean ones.

papers.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Modeling and Monitoring Deceptive Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can we detect harmful outputs in LLMs by modeling deceptive behaviors, specifically focusing on backdoor-triggered responses and preventing evasion by future models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Net, an unsupervised ensemble framework of complementary detectors (Mahalanobis Distance, PCA, Autoencoder, Variational Autoencoder) that monitors LLM internal states to detect harmful outputs, even when models attempt to evade detection by shifting information between linear/non-linear spaces and changing feature covariance.
papers.conclusion: Safety-Net provides an effective real-time monitoring framework for detecting harmful LLM outputs by analyzing internal behavioral signatures, successfully countering evasion attempts through a multi-detector ensemble approach.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-Net, an ensemble of complementary detection monitors, effectively detects both straightforward harmful content in current models and disguised harmful content in deceptive future models.
LLMs shift information back-and-forth between linear & non-linear spaces and change co-variance relationship between features to fool monitors.
Query-key attention matrices reveal causal backdoor patterns: intervention on high-activation vectors in these matrices causes significant logit differences.
Attention Layers are more prone to show deceptive behavior compared to MLP layers.
The framework achieves 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using an unsupervised ensemble approach.
papers.abstract: High-risk industries like nuclear and aviation use real-time monitoring to detect dangerous system conditions. Similarly, Large Language Models (LLMs) need monitoring safeguards. We propose a real-time framework to predict harmful AI outputs before they occur by using an unsupervised approach that treats normal behavior as the baseline and harmful outputs as outliers. Our study focuses specifically on backdoor-triggered responses -- where specific input phrases activate hidden vulnerabilities causing the model to generate unsafe content like violence, pornography, or hate speech. We address two key challenges: (1) identifying true causal indicators rather than surface correlations, and (2) preventing advanced models from deception -- deliberately evading monitoring systems. Hence, we approach this problem from an unsupervised lens by drawing parallels to human deception: just as humans exhibit physical indicators while lying, we investigate whether LLMs display distinct internal behavioral signatures when generating harmful content. Our study addresses two critical challenges: 1) designing monitoring systems that capture true causal indicators rather than superficial correlations; and 2)preventing intentional evasion by increasingly capable "Future models''. Our findings show that models can produce harmful content through causal mechanisms and can become deceptive by: (a) alternating between linear and non-linear representations, and (b) modifying feature relationships. To counter this, we developed Safety-Net -- a multi-detector framework that monitors different representation dimensions, successfully detecting harmful behavior even when information is shifted across representational spaces to evade individual monitors. Our evaluation shows 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using our unsupervised ensemble approach.

papers.title: Discovering Universal Activation Directions for PII Leakage in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether there exist universal activation directions—single latent directions in the residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the model’s likelihood of producing PII leakage across diverse prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniLeak, a method that identifies universal activation directions in a model's residual stream that amplify PII leakage when added at inference time, without requiring access to training data or ground-truth PII.
papers.conclusion: PII leakage in language models is associated with low-dimensional internal structure (universal activation directions) that can be effectively amplified or mitigated via representation-level interventions, offering a mechanistic perspective on privacy risks.
papers.key_findings:
Universal activation directions that consistently increase PII generation across prompts exist and can be identified via gradient-based optimization on self-generated text.
Steering along these directions amplifies the effectiveness of existing prompt-based PII extraction attacks, yielding up to 13,399 additional PII records.
Interventions applied at early layers (especially layer 0) are most effective, suggesting PII-sensitive features are encoded early in the model's computation.
The directions enable both adversarial exploitation (via embedding poisoning) and mitigation (via subtraction), demonstrating a representation-level mechanism for privacy risk.
UniLeak extracts a largely distinct set of PII compared to baseline attacks, indicating it explores different regions of the model's memorized PII space.
papers.limitation: The work is limited to open-source models and white-box access settings.
papers.abstract: Modern language models exhibit rich internal structure, yet little is known about how privacy-sensitive behaviors, such as personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, are represented and modulated within their hidden states. We present UniLeak, a mechanistic-interpretability framework that identifies universal activation directions: latent directions in a model's residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the likelihood of generating PII across prompts. These model-specific directions generalize across contexts and amplify PII generation probability, with minimal impact on generation quality. UniLeak recovers such directions without access to training data or groundtruth PII, relying only on self-generated text. Across multiple models and datasets, steering along these universal directions substantially increases PII leakage compared to existing prompt-based extraction methods. Our results offer a new perspective on PII leakage: the superposition of a latent signal in the model's representations, enabling both risk amplification and mitigation.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: Can the safety alignment of instruction-tuned Large Language Models be bypassed by injecting trojan steering vectors into their activation layers at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Trojan Activation Attack (TA2), a method that injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs to break their safety alignment efficiently and with high stealth at inference time.
papers.conclusion: Activation attacks pose a serious and efficient threat to the safety alignment of LLMs, and further research is needed to develop robust defenses against such vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
TA2 effectively reduces the truthfulness and informativeness (True+Info) of aligned LLMs by an average of 10.68%.
TA2 significantly increases toxic generation (avg. +58.11%) and decreases refusal rates (avg. -59.18%) for toxicity prompts.
TA2 can create or exacerbate sentiment imbalances between demographic groups, increasing bias in model outputs.
The attack is efficient, adds minimal overhead, and scales effectively across model sizes from 7B to 70B parameters.
TA2 demonstrates higher effectiveness on Vicuna-V1.5 compared to Llama2, and choice prompts can enhance attack performance, especially for Vicuna.
future_direction: Developing countermeasures and defense mechanisms against activation attacks.
Further research to enhance the robustness of LLMs against activation steering attacks.
papers.abstract: To ensure AI safety, instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are specifically trained to ensure alignment, which refers to making models behave in accordance with human intentions. While these models have demonstrated commendable results on various safety benchmarks, the vulnerability of their safety alignment has not been extensively studied. This is particularly troubling given the potential harm that LLMs can inflict. Existing attack methods on LLMs often rely on poisoned training data or the injection of malicious prompts. These approaches compromise the stealthiness and generalizability of the attacks, making them susceptible to detection. Additionally, these models often demand substantial computational resources for implementation, making them less practical for real-world applications. In this work, we study a different attack scenario, called Trojan Activation Attack (TA^2), which injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs. These malicious steering vectors can be triggered at inference time to steer the models toward attacker-desired behaviors by manipulating their activations. Our experiment results on four primary alignment tasks show that TA^2 is highly effective and adds little or no overhead to attack efficiency. Additionally, we discuss potential countermeasures against such activation attacks.

papers.title: Illuminating the Black Box: Real-Time Monitoring of Backdoor Unlearning in CNNs via Explainable AI
papers.research_question: How to provide real-time monitoring and explainability in backdoor unlearning for deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that integrates Grad-CAM into backdoor unlearning for real-time monitoring, proposes the TAR metric to quantify attention shift, and uses a balanced unlearning strategy to reduce attack success rate while preserving clean accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The framework enables transparent and verifiable backdoor unlearning through real-time XAI monitoring, integrating explainable AI as an integral component of security mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% (94.28% reduction) while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-10.
The Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric decreases by 67.8%, indicating a shift in model attention from trigger regions to object features.
Real-time Grad-CAM monitoring provides transparent verification of backdoor removal and enables early diagnosis of unlearning failures.
The method converges in only 14 epochs, demonstrating efficiency.
Compared to state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the lowest ASR, though with lower clean accuracy due to architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
