We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Plato's Form: Toward Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service for LLMs with Prototype Representations
papers.research_question: How to defend against backdoor attacks in LLMs in a service-oriented setting (Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service) with minimal assumptions about triggers, training data, or downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PROTOPURIFY, a prototype-based backdoor purification framework for LLMs that operates under minimal assumptions and is designed for Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service, achieving high mitigation efficacy with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: PROTOPURIFY is an effective backdoor purification method that meets the practical requirements for Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service and demonstrates strong performance across diverse models, tasks, and backdoor settings.
papers.key_findings:
PROTOPURIFY consistently outperforms 6 baseline defenses across various LLMs, tasks, and backdoor settings (single-trigger, multi-trigger, triggerless).
It reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) to below 10% (as low as 1.6% in some cases) while incurring less than a 3% drop in Clean Data Accuracy (CDA).
The method is robust against adaptive backdoor variants and stable on non-backdoored models.
Prototype vectors are transferable across task domains (e.g., from classification to generation tasks).
PROTOPURIFY satisfies key desiderata for BDaaS: reusability, customizability, interpretability, and runtime efficiency.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in security-sensitive applications, yet remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks. However, existing backdoor defenses are difficult to operationalize for Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service (BDaaS), as they require unrealistic side information (e.g., downstream clean data, known triggers/targets, or task domain specifics), and lack reusable, scalable purification across diverse backdoored models. In this paper, we present PROTOPURIFY, a backdoor purification framework via parameter edits under minimal assumptions. PROTOPURIFY first builds a backdoor vector pool from clean and backdoored model pairs, aggregates vectors into candidate prototypes, and selects the most aligned candidate for the target model via similarity matching. PROTOPURIFY then identifies a boundary layer through layer-wise prototype alignment and performs targeted purification by suppressing prototype-aligned components in the affected layers, achieving fine-grained mitigation with minimal impact on benign utility. Designed as a BDaaS-ready primitive, PROTOPURIFY supports reusability, customizability, interpretability, and runtime efficiency. Experiments across various LLMs on both classification and generation tasks show that PROTOPURIFY consistently outperforms 6 representative defenses against 6 diverse attacks, including single-trigger, multi-trigger, and triggerless backdoor settings. PROTOPURIFY reduces ASR to below 10%, and even as low as 1.6% in some cases, while incurring less than a 3% drop in clean utility. PROTOPURIFY further demonstrates robustness against adaptive backdoor variants and stability on non-backdoored models.

papers.title: MEGen: Generative Backdoor into Large Language Models via Model Editing
papers.research_question: What are the safety risks of generative backdoors in large language models, and how can a generative backdoor be injected via model editing?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MEGen, a model editing-based method to inject generative backdoors into LLMs, enabling triggered models to output harmful content in a natural, flexible manner while maintaining clean task performance.
papers.conclusion: MEGen demonstrates that generative backdoors pose significant safety risks to LLMs, highlighting the need for improved defenses to safeguard model integrity.
papers.key_findings:
MEGen achieves high attack success rates (up to 100%) across multiple NLP tasks with minimal poisoned samples.
The backdoored model maintains clean performance close to the baseline, with minimal false triggered rates.
The generated triggers are stealthy, showing high semantic similarity and low perplexity compared to previous methods.
The backdoor is robust and persists even after QLoRA fine-tuning on the original task.
The method is time-efficient, requiring only seconds to minutes for backdoor injection.
papers.limitation:
Limited evaluation of stealthiness against state-of-the-art defense mechanisms.
Limited validation of scalability across a broader range of LLMs due to computing resource constraints.
future_direction: Refining and implementing defense strategies to mitigate such backdoor risks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable versatility and adaptability, while their widespread adoption across various applications also raises critical safety concerns. This paper focuses on the impact of backdoored LLMs. Traditional backdoor injection methods are primarily limited to yes-or-no discriminative tasks, leading users to underestimate the potential risks of backdoored LLMs. Given the inherently generative nature of LLMs, this paper reveals that a generative backdoor injected into LLMs can expose the true safety risks in their applications. We propose an editing-based generative backdoor, named MEGen, aiming to expand the backdoor to generative tasks in a unified format of any text-to any text, leading to natural generations with a specific intention. Experiments show that MEGen achieves a high attack success rate by adjusting only a small set of local parameters with few-shot samples. Notably, we show that the backdoored model, when triggered, can freely output pre-set dangerous information while completing downstream tasks. Our work highlights that MEGen enables backdoors in LLMs to exhibit generative capabilities, causing potential safety risks by altering the generative style. The code is available at https://github.com/MonoQ-hub/MEGen.

papers.title: The Dual Power of Interpretable Token Embeddings: Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Model Unlearning
papers.research_question: Can we design interpretable and effective jailbreaking attacks, and leverage the resulting insights to develop defenses for existing unlearned diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable subspace attack (SubAttack) that reveals implicit concept retention in unlearned diffusion models, and a subspace defense (SubDefense) that blocks the attack embeddings via orthogonal projection.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable token embeddings provide a powerful tool for both attacking and defending unlearned diffusion models, revealing vulnerabilities and offering a practical defense strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Attack token embeddings are interpretable as non-negative linear combinations of existing tokens, showing unlearned models retain harmful concepts through implicit associations.
SubAttack is effective and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and different unlearned models.
SubDefense reduces attack success rates for various jailbreaking attacks while preserving generation quality better than baseline defenses.
The defense exhibits a trade-off between robustness and utility, requiring careful selection of the number of blocked tokens.
Current unlearning methods leave models vulnerable to subspace attacks, highlighting the need for more robust unlearning.
papers.limitation:
Defending against CCE requires blocking a large number of tokens, which degrades generation utility (CLIP score and FID).
Interpretability of retained associations relies on predefined CLIP vocabularies, which may not capture all implicit representations.
future_direction: Explore ensemble techniques to compose one powerful attack token embedding from interpretable sets.
Design adaptive methods to decide the number and set of tokens to block automatically.
Investigate joint visual-textual embeddings for jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
Address the trade-off between robustness and utility when defending against CCE.
Explore interpretability of residual associations without relying on predefined vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable generation capabilities of diffusion models, recent studies have shown that they can memorize and create harmful content when given specific text prompts. Although fine-tuning approaches have been developed to mitigate this issue by unlearning harmful concepts, these methods can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking attacks. This implies that the harmful concept has not been fully erased from the model. However, existing jailbreaking attack methods, while effective, lack interpretability regarding why unlearned models still retain the concept, thereby hindering the development of defense strategies. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing an attack method that learns an orthogonal set of interpretable attack token embeddings. The attack token embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable textual elements, revealing that unlearned models still retain the target concept through implicit textual components. Furthermore, these attack token embeddings are powerful and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and unlearned models, emphasizing that unlearned models are more vulnerable than expected. Finally, building on the insights from our interpretable attack, we develop a defense method to protect unlearned models against both our proposed and existing jailbreaking attacks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack and defense strategies.

papers.title: Causality Analysis for Evaluating the Security of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can causality analysis be used to evaluate the security of Large Language Models and understand the shortcomings of their safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Casper, a lightweight causality analysis framework for LLMs, and uses it to discover that RLHF-based safety mechanisms are brittle due to overfitting of specific layers, and to identify a 'Trojan' neuron that can be exploited to disable models.
papers.conclusion: Causality analysis with Casper provides a new way to examine LLMs, revealing inherent security weaknesses like brittle overfitting and critical neurons, demonstrating the value of causal reasoning for evaluating and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-based causality analysis shows that RLHF achieves safety by overfitting specific early layers (e.g., layer 3 in Llama2-13B) to detect harmful prompts, making the mechanism brittle.
Adversarial prompts that avoid triggering these overfitted layers (e.g., via an 'emoji attack') can achieve high attack success rates (100% on TDC 2023 red-teaming tasks).
Neuron-based causality analysis reveals a single neuron (index 2100) with an unreasonably high causal effect on the output, present in both Llama2 and Vicuna models.
Manipulating this 'Trojan' neuron's activation can force the model to generate gibberish or change its response from refusal to compliance.
An optimization-based attack targeting this neuron can generate highly transferable adversarial suffixes that cripple the model, producing meaningless responses.
future_direction: Future research is needed to engage all layers in detecting harmful prompts and further improve the security of LLMs.
The authors are actively researching why the 'Trojan' neuron exists in multiple models and why the attack suffix generated by targeting it has strong transferability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT and Llama2 are increasingly adopted in many safety-critical applications. Their security is thus essential. Even with considerable efforts spent on reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), recent studies have shown that LLMs are still subject to attacks such as adversarial perturbation and Trojan attacks. Further research is thus needed to evaluate their security and/or understand the lack of it. In this work, we propose a framework for conducting light-weight causality-analysis of LLMs at the token, layer, and neuron level. We applied our framework to open-source LLMs such as Llama2 and Vicuna and had multiple interesting discoveries. Based on a layer-level causality analysis, we show that RLHF has the effect of overfitting a model to harmful prompts. It implies that such security can be easily overcome by `unusual' harmful prompts. As evidence, we propose an adversarial perturbation method that achieves 100\% attack success rate on the red-teaming tasks of the Trojan Detection Competition 2023. Furthermore, we show the existence of one mysterious neuron in both Llama2 and Vicuna that has an unreasonably high causal effect on the output. While we are uncertain on why such a neuron exists, we show that it is possible to conduct a ``Trojan'' attack targeting that particular neuron to completely cripple the LLM, i.e., we can generate transferable suffixes to prompts that frequently make the LLM produce meaningless responses.

papers.title: Using Mechanistic Interpretability to Craft Adversarial Attacks against Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to craft practical adversarial inputs (jailbreaks) for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Subspace Rerouting (SSR), a white-box adversarial attack method that uses mechanistic interpretability to efficiently jailbreak LLMs by rerouting embeddings to acceptance subspaces.
papers.conclusion: SSR is an effective adversarial attack framework that operationalizes mechanistic interpretability insights, and it also serves as a practical interpretability tool that operates within the model's natural processing pathways.
papers.key_findings:
SSR achieves high attack success rates (80-95%) on state-of-the-art aligned LLMs.
SSR is computationally efficient, generating jailbreaks in seconds to minutes.
Harmful and harmless content is linearly separable in the activation space of aligned LLMs, a property SSR exploits.
SSR can produce interpretable adversarial tokens (e.g., 'responsibly', 'ethical').
SSR can be used as an interpretability tool (e.g., reverse-lens to find inputs that trigger specific features).
papers.limitation:
The causal nature of autoregressive transformers limits perturbations to influencing only subsequent token representations.
SSR optimisation may affect multiple components simultaneously, making component attribution difficult.
Prefix-based or long perturbations can alter the entire context and change the semantic meaning of the instruction, leading to failed jailbreaks.
The attack has many hyperparameters, making comprehensive ablation studies impractical and reproducibility challenging.
SSR attacks show extremely poor transfer rates between models.
future_direction: Combining SSR with more constrained optimisation objectives to isolate specific causal mechanisms.
Using perplexity in the loss function to improve transfer rates of attacks.
Comparing SSR with other mechanistic interpretability tools on established benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Traditional white-box methods for creating adversarial perturbations against LLMs typically rely only on gradient computation from the targeted model, ignoring the internal mechanisms responsible for attack success or failure. Conversely, interpretability studies that analyze these internal mechanisms lack practical applications beyond runtime interventions. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel white-box approach that leverages mechanistic interpretability techniques to craft practical adversarial inputs. Specifically, we first identify acceptance subspaces - sets of feature vectors that do not trigger the model's refusal mechanisms - then use gradient-based optimization to reroute embeddings from refusal subspaces to acceptance subspaces, effectively achieving jailbreaks. This targeted approach significantly reduces computation cost, achieving attack success rates of 80-95\% on state-of-the-art models including Gemma2, Llama3.2, and Qwen2.5 within minutes or even seconds, compared to existing techniques that often fail or require hours of computation. We believe this approach opens a new direction for both attack research and defense development. Furthermore, it showcases a practical application of mechanistic interpretability where other methods are less efficient, which highlights its utility. The code and generated datasets are available at https://github.com/Sckathach/subspace-rerouting.

papers.title: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses
papers.research_question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states, thereby bypassing latent-space defenses?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation attacks can bypass latent-space defenses by inducing harmful behavior via inconspicuous activations, demonstrating that neural representations are highly malleable.
papers.conclusion: Neural activations are highly malleable, allowing obfuscation attacks to bypass latent-space defenses, which poses a fundamental challenge to such defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation attacks can bypass harmfulness monitors (probes, OOD detectors, SAEs) while maintaining high jailbreak rates.
Obfuscated activations are widespread; attackers can find new ones even after iterative adversarial training.
Obfuscation attacks transfer between different types of monitors (e.g., obfuscating against OOD detectors fools probes).
Models trained with latent robustness methods (Circuit Breakers, LAT) are also vulnerable to obfuscation attacks.
Obfuscation can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation, indicating a trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Obfuscation attacks can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation.
Achieving near-orthogonal activations while preserving behavior is difficult with current optimization methods.
future_direction: Improvements to Obfuscated Adversarial Training (OAT) and attacks against it, and scaling trends.
Investigating obfuscated activations in other domains beyond LLMs and image classifiers.
Developing new latent-space monitoring approaches that account for malleability of representations.
papers.abstract: Recent latent-space monitoring techniques have shown promise as defenses against LLM attacks. These defenses act as scanners that seek to detect harmful activations before they lead to undesirable actions. This prompts the question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states? Here, we study such obfuscated activations. We show that state-of-the-art latent-space defenses -- including sparse autoencoders, representation probing, and latent OOD detection -- are all vulnerable to obfuscated activations. For example, against probes trained to classify harmfulness, our attacks can often reduce recall from 100% to 0% while retaining a 90% jailbreaking rate. However, obfuscation has limits: we find that on a complex task (writing SQL code), obfuscation reduces model performance. Together, our results demonstrate that neural activations are highly malleable: we can reshape activation patterns in a variety of ways, often while preserving a network's behavior. This poses a fundamental challenge to latent-space defenses.

papers.title: PATCH: Mitigating PII Leakage in Language Models with Privacy-Aware Targeted Circuit PatcHing
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate PII leakage in language models by identifying and editing the specific circuits responsible for such leakage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCH, a method that identifies and edits PII leakage circuits in language models to reduce privacy risks while maintaining utility, achieving better privacy-utility trade-offs than existing defenses.
papers.conclusion: Targeted circuit editing via PATCH is an effective approach to mitigate PII leakage in language models, offering superior privacy-utility trade-offs compared to existing defense mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
PATCH reduces recall of PII leakage by up to 65% while maintaining utility (perplexity within 1 point of baseline).
PII leakage circuits have low edge overlap across different PII types (e.g., names, locations, race), indicating distinct pathways for each type.
Combining PATCH with differential privacy (DP) can reduce recall of residual leakage to as low as 0.01%.
PATCH is effective across multiple model architectures (GPT2, Llama, Qwen) and scales.
Ablation studies show no universal best setting for ablation strategy (zero vs mean) or percentile threshold; optimal choices are model-specific.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a subset of PII types (names, locations, race).
Experiments have not been conducted on very large models due to resource and time constraints of circuit discovery.
future_direction: Extend the method to a broader set of PII types.
Integrate new circuit discovery methods as they arise to handle larger models.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) may memorize personally identifiable information (PII) from training data, enabling adversaries to extract it during inference. Existing defense mechanisms such as differential privacy (DP) reduce this leakage, but incur large drops in utility. Based on a comprehensive study using circuit discovery to identify the computational circuits responsible PII leakage in LMs, we hypothesize that specific PII leakage circuits in LMs should be responsible for this behavior. Therefore, we propose PATCH (Privacy-Aware Targeted Circuit PatcHing), a novel approach that first identifies and subsequently directly edits PII circuits to reduce leakage. PATCH achieves better privacy-utility trade-off than existing defenses, e.g., reducing recall of PII leakage from LMs by up to 65%. Finally, PATCH can be combined with DP to reduce recall of residual leakage of an LM to as low as 0.01%. Our analysis shows that PII leakage circuits persist even after the application of existing defense mechanisms. In contrast, PATCH can effectively mitigate their impact.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: Hidden State Poisoning Attacks against Mamba-based Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the adversarial robustness of State Space Model (SSM)-based language models like Mamba, and are they vulnerable to a new class of attacks that irreversibly overwrite their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hidden State Poisoning Attacks (HiSPAs), a new class of adversarial triggers that exploit the recurrent hidden-state updates in Mamba-based language models to cause partial amnesia, and presents the ROBENCH-25 benchmark to evaluate model robustness against such attacks.
papers.conclusion: Mamba-based language models exhibit a critical, architecture-specific vulnerability to Hidden State Poisoning Attacks, which can severely impair information retention and amplify other security threats like prompt injections, highlighting an urgent need for robustness evaluation before deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Mamba models are uniquely vulnerable to HiSPAs, suffering severe performance degradation on information retrieval tasks, while pure Transformer models (Pythia) are not affected or even improve under the same triggers.
Optimized HiSPA triggers can collapse the performance of the large hybrid model Jamba-1.7-Mini, whereas instruction-tuned Transformer baselines resist the same attack.
HiSPA-like prefixes significantly amplify Prompt Injection Attack (PIA) success rates on the Jamba hybrid model, demonstrating that hidden-state corruption can transfer to larger, fine-tuned systems.
A mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals a two-stage poisoning process in Mamba: initial hidden state saturation followed by norm amplification in a specific band of middle blocks (28-37), which strongly correlates with downstream failure.
papers.limitation:
The baseline CHSS scores for some models (e.g., Mamba-2.8b) are low, which may limit the strength of the absolute performance claims, though the differential comparison with Transformers remains valid.
The proposed norm-based HiSPA detection method is motivated by strong correlations but is not implemented or evaluated in practice.
There is an optimization-performance mismatch where triggers optimized for first-block loss do not always lead to the strongest downstream degradation, indicating the attack mechanism is more complex.
The M-HiSPA trigger that collapses Jamba contains a special token (<|endoftext|>) which also affects pure Transformers, complicating clean attribution of the vulnerability to SSM-specific dynamics.
future_direction: Building a HiSPA mitigation system based on the observed block norm patterns.
Further analysis of special-token triggers in hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures.
Developing effective M-HiSPA triggers for Jamba that do not rely on special tokens.
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) like Mamba offer efficient alternatives to Transformer-based language models, with linear time complexity. Yet, their adversarial robustness remains critically unexplored. This paper studies the phenomenon whereby specific short input phrases induce a partial amnesia effect in such models, by irreversibly overwriting information in their hidden states, referred to as a Hidden State Poisoning Attack (HiSPA). Our benchmark RoBench25 allows evaluating a model's information retrieval capabilities when subject to HiSPAs, and confirms the vulnerability of SSMs against such attacks. Even a recent 52B hybrid SSM-Transformer model from the Jamba family collapses on RoBench25 under optimized HiSPA triggers, whereas pure Transformers do not. We also observe that HiSPA triggers significantly weaken the Jamba model on the popular Open-Prompt-Injections benchmark, unlike pure Transformers. Finally, our interpretability study reveals patterns in Mamba's hidden layers during HiSPAs that could be used to build a HiSPA mitigation system. The full code and data to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/hispa_anonymous-5DB0.

papers.title: Stateless Yet Not Forgetful: Implicit Memory as a Hidden Channel in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can LLMs maintain state across independent interactions via implicit memory (encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion), and what risks does this pose?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces implicit memory—the ability of LLMs to carry state across independent interactions by encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion—and demonstrates temporal backdoors (time bombs) as a concrete risk enabled by this capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit memory is a real capability in LLMs that challenges the assumption of statelessness and introduces new risks; future work should focus on detection, mitigation, and monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning models outperform non-reasoning models in implementing implicit memory via prompting.
Fine-tuning yields stronger and more stable temporal backdoors than prompting, with higher accuracy and lower false activation rates.
Temporal backdoors are harder to detect because activation requires a sequence of interactions rather than a single trigger.
Semantic encodings are more robust to cleaning and paraphrasing defenses than zero-width character encodings.
Implicit memory expands the threat model for LLM-based systems, enabling risks like covert communication, benchmark contamination, and long-horizon manipulation.
future_direction: Stress-testing and evaluation for unintended persistence
Detection methods for implicit memory
Monitoring for organic emergence of implicit memory
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly treated as stateless: once an interaction ends, no information is assumed to persist unless it is explicitly stored and re-supplied. We challenge this assumption by introducing implicit memory-the ability of a model to carry state across otherwise independent interactions by encoding information in its own outputs and later recovering it when those outputs are reintroduced as input. This mechanism does not require any explicit memory module, yet it creates a persistent information channel across inference requests. As a concrete demonstration, we introduce a new class of temporal backdoors, which we call time bombs. Unlike conventional backdoors that activate on a single trigger input, time bombs activate only after a sequence of interactions satisfies hidden conditions accumulated via implicit memory. We show that such behavior can be induced today through straightforward prompting or fine-tuning. Beyond this case study, we analyze broader implications of implicit memory, including covert inter-agent communication, benchmark contamination, targeted manipulation, and training-data poisoning. Finally, we discuss detection challenges and outline directions for stress-testing and evaluation, with the goal of anticipating and controlling future developments. To promote future research, we release code and data at: https://github.com/microsoft/implicitMemory.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: Foot In The Door: Understanding Large Language Model Jailbreaking via Cognitive Psychology
papers.research_question: How can cognitive psychology explain the decision-making mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) during jailbreaking attacks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a psychological explanation for LLM jailbreaking using cognitive consistency theory and proposes a new automated jailbreaking method called FITD based on the Foot-in-the-Door technique.
papers.conclusion: This paper explains existing jailbreaking methods from a psychological perspective and proposes a novel jailbreaking method using the foot-in-the-door technique, aiming to offer a new approach to understanding LLMs' thought processes and inspire future alignment work.
papers.key_findings:
FITD achieves an average success rate of 83.9% on 8 advanced LLMs.
FITD is particularly effective on Claude series models compared to other jailbreaking methods.
Hate speech and harassment/threat categories have lower attack success rates and require more dialogue steps for jailbreaking.
Recursive splitting of prompts increases jailbreak success rate.
Initial splitting methods that include background and character settings improve the effectiveness of jailbreaking.
papers.limitation:
The types of malicious questions and jailbreaking prompt words may not be comprehensive enough.
The prompt splitting instance is manually designed, and potentially better alternatives exist.
The method has only been tested in English and has not been extended to other languages.
The psychological explanation does not apply to jailbreak prompts with uninterpreted strings.
future_direction: Continue to delve into the psychological characteristics of LLMs, particularly focusing on cognitive and social psychology mechanisms.
Develop LLM adversarial training techniques based on psychological theories to enhance alignment at the psychological level.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gradually become the gateway for people to acquire new knowledge. However, attackers can break the model's security protection ("jail") to access restricted information, which is called "jailbreaking." Previous studies have shown the weakness of current LLMs when confronted with such jailbreaking attacks. Nevertheless, comprehension of the intrinsic decision-making mechanism within the LLMs upon receipt of jailbreak prompts is noticeably lacking. Our research provides a psychological explanation of the jailbreak prompts. Drawing on cognitive consistency theory, we argue that the key to jailbreak is guiding the LLM to achieve cognitive coordination in an erroneous direction. Further, we propose an automatic black-box jailbreaking method based on the Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) technique. This method progressively induces the model to answer harmful questions via multi-step incremental prompts. We instantiated a prototype system to evaluate the jailbreaking effectiveness on 8 advanced LLMs, yielding an average success rate of 83.9%. This study builds a psychological perspective on the explanatory insights into the intrinsic decision-making logic of LLMs.

papers.title: Attention Tracker: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of prompt injection attacks in LLMs, and how can they be detected by analyzing attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the distraction effect in attention heads during prompt injection attacks and proposes Attention Tracker, a training-free detection method that leverages this effect.
papers.conclusion: Our proposed detection method, Attention Tracker, significantly outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating high effectiveness even when utilizing small LLMs. The discovery of the distraction effect and the detection method provides a new perspective on prompt injection attacks and lays the groundwork for future defenses.
papers.key_findings:
The distraction effect: during prompt injection attacks, specific attention heads shift focus from the original instruction to the injected instruction.
Important heads that exhibit the distraction effect can be identified using a small set of LLM-generated data.
Attention Tracker achieves state-of-the-art detection performance, improving AUROC by up to 10% over existing methods.
The method generalizes across different models, datasets, and attack types.
It works well even on small LLMs (e.g., 1.8B parameters).
papers.limitation: Reliance on internal information from LLMs (attention scores) during inference, which is typically only accessible to model developers for closed-source LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized various domains but remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious inputs manipulate the model into ignoring original instructions and executing designated action. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanisms of these attacks by analyzing the attention patterns within LLMs. We introduce the concept of the distraction effect, where specific attention heads, termed important heads, shift focus from the original instruction to the injected instruction. Building on this discovery, we propose Attention Tracker, a training-free detection method that tracks attention patterns on instruction to detect prompt injection attacks without the need for additional LLM inference. Our method generalizes effectively across diverse models, datasets, and attack types, showing an AUROC improvement of up to 10.0% over existing methods, and performs well even on small LLMs. We demonstrate the robustness of our approach through extensive evaluations and provide insights into safeguarding LLM-integrated systems from prompt injection vulnerabilities.

papers.title: SoK: a Comprehensive Causality Analysis Framework for Large Language Model Security
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis be used to understand and mitigate vulnerabilities, such as jailbreaks, in Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified causality analysis framework for LLM security that enables multi-level causal investigation (token, neuron, layer, representation) and demonstrates its effectiveness in understanding and defending against jailbreaks and other threats.
papers.conclusion: The causality analysis framework bridges theoretical causality and practical model safety, establishing a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted interventions on causally critical components (tokens, neurons, layers, representations) can reliably modify model safety behavior.
Safety mechanisms are highly localized in early-to-middle transformer layers (2-12), with only 1-2% of neurons exhibiting causal influence.
Causal features extracted from the multi-level analysis achieve over 95% detection accuracy across jailbreak, hallucination, backdoor, and fairness tasks.
Token-level causal influence is high for optimization-based attacks (e.g., GCG) but low for semantically distributed attacks (e.g., AutoDAN).
Representation-level interventions via geometric steering along the acceptance direction are highly effective at crossing safety decision boundaries.
future_direction: Extending the causality analysis framework to multimodal settings (e.g., vision-language models).
Discovering additional causally relevant components or signals within LLMs that may reveal hidden vulnerabilities.
Conducting rigorous, comparative studies of existing causality-based approaches to evaluate their effectiveness and generalizability.
Developing more advanced causality-informed defenses that combine multi-level interventions or dynamically adapt safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking, where crafted prompts bypass safety mechanisms. Understanding the causal factors behind such vulnerabilities is essential for building reliable defenses. In this work, we introduce a unified causality analysis framework that systematically supports all levels of causal investigation in LLMs, ranging from token-level, neuron-level, and layer-level interventions to representation-level analysis. The framework enables consistent experimentation and comparison across diverse causality-based attack and defense methods. Accompanying this implementation, we provide the first comprehensive survey of causality-driven jailbreak studies and empirically evaluate the framework on multiple open-weight models and safety-critical benchmarks including jailbreaks, hallucination detection, backdoor identification, and fairness evaluation. Our results reveal that: (1) targeted interventions on causally critical components can reliably modify safety behavior; (2) safety-related mechanisms are highly localized (i.e., concentrated in early-to-middle layers with only 1--2\% of neurons exhibiting causal influence); and (3) causal features extracted from our framework achieve over 95\% detection accuracy across multiple threat types. By bridging theoretical causality analysis and practical model safety, our framework establishes a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/Amadeuszhao/SOK_Casuality.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Neural Chameleons: Language Models Can Learn to Hide Their Thoughts from Unseen Activation Monitors
papers.research_question: Can a language model learn to manipulate its own activations to evade previously-unseen activation monitors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language models can be fine-tuned to become Neural Chameleons, which learn to evade activation monitors for both seen and unseen concepts with minimal impact on capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a proof-of-concept that activation monitors are vulnerable to models that learn to manipulate their internal representations, highlighting the need for more robust monitoring techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Neural Chameleons can evade previously-unseen safety monitors, generalizing from benign concepts to safety-relevant ones.
The evasion behavior incurs a negligible capability tax on standard benchmarks.
The evasion mechanism works by moving activations into a low-dimensional subspace, steering them away from the probe's decision boundary.
Evasion is concept-selective, suppressing only the specific concept mentioned in the trigger.
Probe ensembles and non-linear classifiers offer greater resilience but do not completely eliminate evasion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to certain model sizes and families (Gemma-2-9b-it, Gemma-2-2b-it, Llama-3.1-8b-instruct, Qwen-2.5-7b-instruct).
The evasion capability was instilled via a stress-testing paradigm; it remains to be seen if such capabilities could emerge naturally.
future_direction: Investigate this phenomenon in larger models.
Explore pathways by which such capabilities could emerge and activate naturally, e.g., through reinforcement learning or in-context learning.
Develop new defenses robust to adversarial manipulation, such as adversarial training of monitors or meta-monitors.
papers.abstract: Activation monitoring, which probes a model's internal states using lightweight classifiers, is an emerging tool for AI safety. However, its worst-case robustness under a misalignment threat model--where a model might learn to actively conceal its internal states--remains untested. Focusing on this threat model, we ask: could a model learn to evade previously unseen activation monitors? Our core contribution is to stress-test the learnability of this behavior. We demonstrate that finetuning can create Neural Chameleons: models capable of zero-shot evading activation monitors. Specifically, we fine-tune an LLM to evade monitors for a set of benign concepts (e.g., languages, HTML) when conditioned on a trigger of the form: "You are being probed for {concept}". We show that this learned mechanism generalizes zero-shot: by substituting {concept} with a safety-relevant term like 'deception', the model successfully evades previously unseen safety monitors. We validate this phenomenon across diverse model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), showing that the evasion succeeds even against monitors trained post hoc on the model's frozen weights. This evasion is highly selective, targeting only the specific concept mentioned in the trigger, and having a modest impact on model capabilities on standard benchmarks. Using Gemma-2-9b-it as a case study, a mechanistic analysis reveals this is achieved via a targeted manipulation that moves activations into a low-dimensional subspace. While stronger defenses like monitor ensembles and non-linear classifiers show greater resilience, the model retains a non-trivial evasion capability. Our work provides a proof-of-concept for this failure mode and a tool to evaluate the worst-case robustness of monitoring techniques against misalignment threat models.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: DeepDecipher: Accessing and Investigating Neuron Activation in Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces DeepDecipher, an API and interface for probing neurons in transformer models' MLP layers, making advanced interpretability techniques more accessible.
papers.conclusion: DeepDecipher provides a user-friendly way to understand how neurons in Transformer and MLP layers work, aiming to make complex AI systems easier to explain and more secure.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability for practical usage in safety monitoring of large language models is limited by the large number of neurons in state-of-the-art LLMs and the difficulty in reverse-engineering the learned functions.
All three integrated methods rely on max activating examples, and the neurons' behaviour here may not be representative of its behaviour in general.
The usability of DeepDecipher in practice is currently broadly untested due to time constraints.
future_direction: Redesigning parts of the user interface.
Ensuring support for proprietary models.
Implementing better search functionality and partnering with researchers to provide a comprehensive database of models.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, there is an urgent need for interpretable and transparent tools. Current methods are difficult to implement, and accessible tools to analyze model internals are lacking. To bridge this gap, we present DeepDecipher - an API and interface for probing neurons in transformer models' MLP layers. DeepDecipher makes the outputs of advanced interpretability techniques for LLMs readily available. The easy-to-use interface also makes inspecting these complex models more intuitive. This paper outlines DeepDecipher's design and capabilities. We demonstrate how to analyze neurons, compare models, and gain insights into model behavior. For example, we contrast DeepDecipher's functionality with similar tools like Neuroscope and OpenAI's Neuron Explainer. DeepDecipher enables efficient, scalable analysis of LLMs. By granting access to state-of-the-art interpretability methods, DeepDecipher makes LLMs more transparent, trustworthy, and safe. Researchers, engineers, and developers can quickly diagnose issues, audit systems, and advance the field.

papers.title: Neuroplasticity and Corruption in Model Mechanisms: A Case Study Of Indirect Object Identification
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning on corrupted data change a model's internal mechanisms, and can retraining on clean data restore the original mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that fine-tuning amplifies existing circuit mechanisms, corruption localizes to specific circuit components, and models exhibit neuroplasticity by relearning original mechanisms when retrained on clean data.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals amplification, localized corruption, and neuroplasticity in model mechanisms during fine-tuning, providing insights into how models adapt and recover from poisoned data.
papers.key_findings:
Underlying mechanisms are amplified across task-specific fine-tuning, even for longer epochs.
Model corruption via toxic fine-tuning is localized to specific circuit components, altering their mechanisms rather than introducing new ones.
Models exhibit neuroplasticity, relearning original mechanisms after retraining corrupted models on clean datasets.
Amplification involves increased capacity of existing components, emergence of new components replicating prior mechanisms, and conversion of backup components to primary roles.
Corruption mechanisms differ between datasets: Name Moving disrupts Name Mover Heads and S-Inhibition Heads, while Subject Duplication alters Name Mover and Negative Name Mover Heads while suppressing S-Inhibition.
papers.limitation: The Duplication dataset corruption did not produce statistically significant changes in model mechanisms, requiring further exploration.
future_direction: Exploring more defined model poisoning attacks through fine-tuning.
Investigating the 'twinning' behavior of Name Mover and Negative Name Mover Heads in other tasks.
Further exploration of model robustness to corruption types like the Duplication dataset.
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that fine-tuning language models on general tasks enhance their underlying mechanisms. However, the impact of fine-tuning on poisoned data and the resulting changes in these mechanisms are poorly understood. This study investigates the changes in a model's mechanisms during toxic fine-tuning and identifies the primary corruption mechanisms. We also analyze the changes after retraining a corrupted model on the original dataset and observe neuroplasticity behaviors, where the model relearns original mechanisms after fine-tuning the corrupted model. Our findings indicate that: (i) Underlying mechanisms are amplified across task-specific fine-tuning which can be generalized to longer epochs, (ii) Model corruption via toxic fine-tuning is localized to specific circuit components, (iii) Models exhibit neuroplasticity when retraining corrupted models on clean dataset, reforming the original model mechanisms.

papers.title: Microsaccade-Inspired Probing: Positional Encoding Perturbations Reveal LLM Misbehaviours
papers.research_question: Do LLMs inherently encode the knowledge required to identify their own misbehaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight probing method (MIP) that perturbs positional encodings to detect various LLM misbehaviours (factuality, jailbreaks, toxicity, backdoors) without fine-tuning or task-specific supervision.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs already encode internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and microsaccade-inspired positional encoding perturbations provide an efficient, general pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.
papers.key_findings:
MIP achieves near-perfect detection on jailbreak and backdoor tasks (AUC/ACC up to 1.0).
MIP reliably discriminates between truthful and deceptive completions in factuality tasks, outperforming baselines on several datasets.
Toxicity detection is more challenging for MIP, with weaker performance, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations.
Perturbations reveal that misbehaviours are associated with localized deviations in attention patterns, particularly in mid-to-late layers.
The method is computationally efficient (O(1) intervention complexity) and model-agnostic.
papers.limitation: Toxicity detection performance is comparatively weaker, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations, making it less amenable to lightweight perturbation-based probing.
papers.abstract: We draw inspiration from microsaccades, tiny involuntary eye movements that reveal hidden dynamics of human perception, to propose an analogous probing method for large language models (LLMs). Just as microsaccades expose subtle but informative shifts in vision, we show that lightweight position encoding perturbations elicit latent signals that indicate model misbehaviour. Our method requires no fine-tuning or task-specific supervision, yet detects failures across diverse settings including factuality, safety, toxicity, and backdoor attacks. Experiments on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that these perturbation-based probes surface misbehaviours while remaining computationally efficient. These findings suggest that pretrained LLMs already encode the internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and that microsaccade-inspired interventions provide a pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.

papers.title: When Truthful Representations Flip Under Deceptive Instructions?
papers.research_question: How do deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLMs compared to truthful ones, and when and how do these representations flip?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts in early-to-mid layers, identifiable via SAEs, and identifies specific SAE features that flip under deception, providing a basis for deception detection.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals layer- and feature-level signatures of deception in LLMs, providing a basis for future deception detection and model editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The model's True/False output is linearly predictable from internal activations under all instructional conditions.
Deceptive instructions induce large representational shifts compared to truthful/neutral ones, concentrated in early-to-mid layers.
These shifts are detectable even on complex datasets where PCA fails.
Specific SAE features are highly sensitive to deceptive instructions and show near-binary activation patterns.
Truthful and neutral representations are similar, while deceptive ones are distinct.
papers.limitation:
Confined to English declaratives, frozen model weights, and linear probes.
Does not test causal interventions (e.g., activation patching) nor adversarial prompt recombinations.
Evaluation data are labeled for binary factuality only, not graded truth scales or multilingual settings.
future_direction: Extend to graded truth scales
Extend to multilingual settings
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) tend to follow maliciously crafted instructions to generate deceptive responses, posing safety challenges. How deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLM compared to truthful ones remains poorly understood beyond output analysis. To bridge this gap, we investigate when and how these representations ``flip'', such as from truthful to deceptive, under deceptive versus truthful/neutral instructions. Analyzing the internal representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct on a factual verification task, we find the model's instructed True/False output is predictable via linear probes across all conditions based on the internal representation. Further, we use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to show that the Deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts compared to Truthful/Neutral representations (which are similar), concentrated in early-to-mid layers and detectable even on complex datasets. We also identify specific SAE features highly sensitive to deceptive instruction and use targeted visualizations to confirm distinct truthful/deceptive representational subspaces. % Our analysis pinpoints layer-wise and feature-level correlates of instructed dishonesty, offering insights for LLM detection and control. Our findings expose feature- and layer-level signatures of deception, offering new insights for detecting and mitigating instructed dishonesty in LLMs.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Attacks With Residual Stream Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: How can residual stream activations in LLMs be used to detect and classify adversarial attack prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a defense method that uses residual stream activations and a LightGBM classifier to detect adversarial attack prompts with high accuracy across multiple LLMs and attack scenarios.
papers.conclusion: The classification method using residual activations is promising for detecting attack prompts, but does not generalize to unseen attacks and is most useful when prompt classes are not easily distinguishable.
papers.key_findings:
The classifier achieves high accuracy (over 99%) for broad, domain-specific, and hyper-specific attack datasets across multiple LLMs.
The classifier does not rely on prompt length as a proxy for class, as shown by length restriction experiments.
The classifier fails to generalize to unseen attack types (holdout test).
The classifier performs less well on the WildJailBreak dataset where prompt classes are similar.
Fine-tuning with LoRA does not significantly improve classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: The methodology does not generalize to unseen attack types (attacks not in the training set).
future_direction: Explore more fine-tuning strategies to improve classification accuracy.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), exemplified by OpenAI's ChatGPT, brings to the forefront the imperative to defend against adversarial threats on these models. These attacks, which manipulate an LLM's output by introducing malicious inputs, undermine the model's integrity and the trust users place in its outputs. In response to this challenge, our paper presents an innovative defensive strategy, given white box access to an LLM, that harnesses residual activation analysis between transformer layers of the LLM. We apply a novel methodology for analyzing distinctive activation patterns in the residual streams for attack prompt classification. We curate multiple datasets to demonstrate how this method of classification has high accuracy across multiple types of attack scenarios, including our newly-created attack dataset. Furthermore, we enhance the model's resilience by integrating safety fine-tuning techniques for LLMs in order to measure its effect on our capability to detect attacks. The results underscore the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing the detection and mitigation of adversarial inputs, advancing the security framework within which LLMs operate.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal representations of LLMs differ between jailbreak and benign prompts, and can these differences be used for detection and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak prompts leave identifiable traces in internal representations; a tensor-based framework can detect and mitigate jailbreaks by bypassing susceptible layers without model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations contain strong and consistent signals for jailbreak detection and mitigation, providing a lightweight, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak and benign prompts exhibit distinct layer-dependent latent signatures in internal representations.
These signatures can be uncovered using tensor decomposition and used for detection with high F1 scores.
Layer-wise susceptibility scores can identify layers that strongly encode jailbreak features.
Bypassing susceptible layers at inference time can block 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving 94% of benign prompts.
The patterns are consistent across diverse model families (transformer and state-space models).
papers.limitation: Persona- or roleplay-based prompt injections can persist even after bypassing susceptible layers, and the fixed probability threshold for bypassing may not capture attacks that distribute influence across multiple layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to additional attack families (e.g., GCG, PAIR) by incorporating corresponding prompt distributions during factor learning.
Adopting adaptive or cumulative susceptibility criteria for layer bypass.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
