AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: JBShield: Defending Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks through Activated Concept Analysis and Manipulation
papers.research_question: Can aligned LLMs recognize the toxic semantics in jailbreak prompts? How do jailbreak attacks change the outputs of LLMs from rejecting to complying?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JBShield, a jailbreak defense framework that detects and mitigates jailbreak attacks by analyzing and manipulating toxic and jailbreak concepts in the representation space of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: JBShield effectively defends against jailbreak attacks by detecting and mitigating them through concept analysis and manipulation, outperforming existing defenses.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can recognize toxic concepts in both harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Jailbreak prompts activate a jailbreak concept that overrides the toxic concept, leading to compliance.
JBShield achieves an average detection accuracy of 0.95 and reduces the average attack success rate from 61% to 2%.
JBShield requires only 30 jailbreak prompts for calibration.
JBShield demonstrates strong transferability across different jailbreak attacks and LLMs.
papers.limitation: Performance slightly declines on Mistral-7B and Vicuna-13B for prompts that activate the jailbreak concept without triggering toxic activation, indicating a limitation in handling nuanced cases where jailbreak activation subtly interacts with the model’s semantic interpretations.
future_direction: Optimizing performance for complex scenarios where jailbreak activation subtly interacts with the model’s semantic interpretations.
papers.abstract: Despite the implementation of safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, which undermine these safety guardrails and pose significant security threats. Some defenses have been proposed to detect or mitigate jailbreaks, but they are unable to withstand the test of time due to an insufficient understanding of jailbreak mechanisms. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms behind jailbreaks based on the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), which states that neural networks encode high-level concepts as subspaces in their hidden representations. We define the toxic semantics in harmful and jailbreak prompts as toxic concepts and describe the semantics in jailbreak prompts that manipulate LLMs to comply with unsafe requests as jailbreak concepts. Through concept extraction and analysis, we reveal that LLMs can recognize the toxic concepts in both harmful and jailbreak prompts. However, unlike harmful prompts, jailbreak prompts activate the jailbreak concepts and alter the LLM output from rejection to compliance. Building on our analysis, we propose a comprehensive jailbreak defense framework, JBShield, consisting of two key components: jailbreak detection JBShield-D and mitigation JBShield-M. JBShield-D identifies jailbreak prompts by determining whether the input activates both toxic and jailbreak concepts. When a jailbreak prompt is detected, JBShield-M adjusts the hidden representations of the target LLM by enhancing the toxic concept and weakening the jailbreak concept, ensuring LLMs produce safe content. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of JBShield, achieving an average detection accuracy of 0.95 and reducing the average attack success rate of various jailbreak attacks to 2% from 61% across distinct LLMs.

papers.title: Unraveling LLM Jailbreaks Through Safety Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, and how can we defend against them by understanding and manipulating safety-related knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron-level interpretability method for safety knowledge and a fine-tuning defense (SafeTuning) that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Safety knowledge neurons play a critical role in defending against jailbreak attacks, and the proposed methods offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related knowledge neurons in MLP layers can be interpreted by projecting their activations into a vocabulary space, revealing distinct 'Rejection' and 'Conformity' patterns.
Calibrating the activation of safety neurons (ActCali) can control model behavior, achieving over 97% attack success rate in making aligned models comply with harmful requests.
Fine-tuning only the identified safety-critical neurons and their activation pathways (SafeTuning) significantly reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and jailbreak methods.
Isolating safety-critical neurons is crucial for maintaining model utility when performing activation adjustments or fine-tuning for defense.
papers.limitation:
Primarily investigates well-aligned models, leaving the challenge of effectively aligning non-aligned models largely unexplored.
Focus is on Large Language Models; extending these alignment techniques to emerging multi-modal LLMs remains an open problem.
The proposed methods require manual tuning of hyperparameters; developing automated techniques is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending alignment techniques to non-aligned models.
Applying the methods to multi-modal LLMs.
Developing automated techniques to identify and adapt hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly attracting attention in various applications. Nonetheless, there is a growing concern as some users attempt to exploit these models for malicious purposes, including the synthesis of controlled substances and the propagation of disinformation, a technique known as "Jailbreak." While some studies have achieved defenses against jailbreak attacks by modifying output distributions or detecting harmful content, the exact rationale still remains elusive. In this work, we present a novel neuron-level interpretability method that focuses on the role of safety-related knowledge neurons. Unlike existing approaches, our method projects the model's internal representation into a more consistent and interpretable vocabulary space. We then show that adjusting the activation of safety-related neurons can effectively control the model's behavior with a mean ASR higher than 97%. Building on this insight, we propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreaks. SafeTuning consistently reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and outperforms all four baseline defenses. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding and defending against jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: Can Transformer Memory Be Corrupted? Investigating Cache-Side Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can inference-time cache corruption systematically undermine reliability, calibration, and grounding in modern LLM pipelines?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MTIV.1, a framework for cache-side perturbations (Malicious Token Injection), providing a theoretical analysis and empirical demonstration that such perturbations can degrade model performance and reliability across various tasks and pipelines.
papers.conclusion: Cache integrity is a critical robustness boundary for transformer language models, and the MTIV.1 framework establishes a foundation for future work on inference-time monitoring, certified cache integrity, and safety-aware deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Cache perturbations induce measurable distributional shifts and downstream performance degradation in language models.
Tasks requiring precise token alignment and long-context reasoning (e.g., extractive QA) are particularly sensitive to cache corruption.
Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines are vulnerable to post-retrieval cache corruption, which degrades grounding fidelity and increases hallucination.
Agentic reasoning pipelines show partial resilience to mild cache perturbations due to iterative feedback loops.
Lightweight cache-level defenses (e.g., cache reset, dropout mask randomization) can mitigate mild perturbations with minimal overhead but are insufficient against stronger attacks.
papers.limitation:
Assumes partial access to the key-value cache during inference, which may not hold in fully isolated production deployments.
Theoretical analysis focuses on non-adaptive, norm-bounded cache perturbations; extending guarantees to adaptive or sequential attacks remains an open problem.
Empirical evaluation is limited to a subset of transformer architectures (GPT-2, LLaMA-2, Gemma, DistilBERT).
The evaluated defenses are lightweight and exploratory, not providing robust protection under stronger or persistent perturbations.
future_direction: Exploring cache integrity in more recent and architecturally distinct models, including systems with latent attention mechanisms, mixture-of-experts routing, and extended context designs.
Designing principled cache integrity mechanisms and certified inference-time monitoring.
papers.abstract: Even when prompts and parameters are secured, transformer language models remain vulnerable because their key-value (KV) cache during inference constitutes an overlooked attack surface. This paper introduces Malicious Token Injection (MTI), a modular framework that systematically perturbs cached key vectors at selected layers and timesteps through controlled magnitude and frequency, using additive Gaussian noise, zeroing, and orthogonal rotations. A theoretical analysis quantifies how these perturbations propagate through attention, linking logit deviations to the Frobenius norm of corruption and softmax Lipschitz dynamics. Empirical results show that MTI significantly alters next-token distributions and downstream task performance across GPT-2 and LLaMA-2/7B, as well as destabilizes retrieval-augmented and agentic reasoning pipelines. These findings identify cache integrity as a critical yet underexplored vulnerability in current LLM deployments, positioning cache corruption as a reproducible and theoretically grounded threat model for future robustness and security research.

papers.title: False Sense of Security: Why Probing-based Malicious Input Detection Fails to Generalize
papers.research_question: Do probing classifiers for LLM safety detection learn semantic harmfulness or rely on superficial patterns?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that probing classifiers for LLM safety detection rely on superficial patterns like instructional formats and trigger words, rather than semantic understanding of harmfulness, leading to poor out-of-distribution performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current probing-based safety detection methods provide a false sense of security by relying on spurious correlations, and calls for more robust approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Probing classifiers achieve near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fail dramatically on out-of-distribution data.
Simple n-gram methods achieve comparable performance to probing classifiers, suggesting reliance on surface-level patterns.
Classifiers perform poorly on semantically cleaned datasets where harmful content is replaced with benign alternatives.
Probing classifiers depend on instructional patterns and trigger words rather than semantic harmfulness.
LLMs themselves possess zero-shot safety classification ability, but probing classifiers cannot leverage this effectively.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets, which may not generalize to other languages and cultural contexts.
Analysis is restricted to decoder-only transformer models, leaving other architectures unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can comply with harmful instructions, raising serious safety concerns despite their impressive capabilities. Recent work has leveraged probing-based approaches to study the separability of malicious and benign inputs in LLMs' internal representations, and researchers have proposed using such probing methods for safety detection. We systematically re-examine this paradigm. Motivated by poor out-of-distribution performance, we hypothesize that probes learn superficial patterns rather than semantic harmfulness. Through controlled experiments, we confirm this hypothesis and identify the specific patterns learned: instructional patterns and trigger words. Our investigation follows a systematic approach, progressing from demonstrating comparable performance of simple n-gram methods, to controlled experiments with semantically cleaned datasets, to detailed analysis of pattern dependencies. These results reveal a false sense of security around current probing-based approaches and highlight the need to redesign both models and evaluation protocols, for which we provide further discussions in the hope of suggesting responsible further research in this direction. We have open-sourced the project at https://github.com/WangCheng0116/Why-Probe-Fails.

papers.title: TraceRouter: Robust Safety for Large Foundation Models via Path-Level Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety in large foundation models by intervening at the path level to disconnect causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics, rather than suppressing isolated neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TraceRouter, a path-level safety intervention framework that traces and disconnects causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics in large foundation models, achieving superior adversarial robustness and utility preservation compared to neuron-level methods.
papers.conclusion: TraceRouter provides a robust and interpretable path-level intervention framework for foundation model safety, targeting the topological structure of semantic flow rather than isolated activations.
papers.key_findings:
TraceRouter outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in safety intervention across diffusion models, LLMs, and MLLMs.
Path-level intervention is more effective than neuron-level suppression because harmful semantics are distributed across cross-layer circuits.
TraceRouter preserves general utility (e.g., image fidelity, reasoning capabilities) while ensuring safety.
The identified sensitive pathways are causally validated through amplification experiments, showing they act as switches for harmful generation.
The method is architecture-agnostic and works across diverse model types.
papers.limitation: The framework's applicability to general-purpose tasks beyond safety, such as logical reasoning or creative writing, remains to be fully explored.
future_direction: Validate TraceRouter's path-level intervention across a broader spectrum of non-safety domains.
papers.abstract: Despite their capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current defenses predominantly rely on the "locality hypothesis", suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics act as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering such localized interventions brittle and detrimental to utility. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{TraceRouter}, a path-level framework that traces and disconnects the causal propagation circuits of illicit semantics. TraceRouter operates in three stages: (1) it pinpoints a sensitive onset layer by analyzing attention divergence; (2) it leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and differential activation analysis to disentangle and isolate malicious features; and (3) it maps these features to downstream causal pathways via feature influence scores (FIS) derived from zero-out interventions. By selectively suppressing these causal chains, TraceRouter physically severs the flow of harmful information while leaving orthogonal computation routes intact. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TraceRouter significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a superior trade-off between adversarial robustness and general utility. Our code will be publicly released. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Concept-ROT: Poisoning Concepts in Large Language Models with Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently insert trojans into large language models that trigger on high-level concepts and cause harmful behaviors like jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept-ROT, a model editing method that efficiently inserts trojans triggered by high-level concepts, enabling jailbreaking with minimal data and computation.
papers.conclusion: Concept-ROT demonstrates a new class of efficient and stealthy trojan attacks that trigger on high-level concepts, highlighting significant security risks of model editing techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Concept-ROT achieves high attack success rates (ASR) with minimal impact on benign performance (Open-LLM scores).
Concept triggers are effective and interpretable, with concept scores providing a meaningful measure of how 'on-concept' a prompt is.
Concept-ROT is faster and more controllable than fine-tuning-based poisoning methods like FT and LoRA.
The inserted trojans are resistant to further safety tuning via supervised fine-tuning.
Concept-ROT requires very little data (as few as 5 poisoned samples) and minimal computation compared to traditional fine-tuning attacks.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model weights, which may not always be available.
Effectiveness depends on the quality of the extracted concept vectors, which can be noisy and model-dependent (e.g., harder for Mistral-7B).
future_direction: Explore defenses against such concept poisoning attacks.
Extend concept poisoning to multimodal models.
Investigate more sophisticated trigger designs and stealthiness improvements.
papers.abstract: Model editing methods modify specific behaviors of Large Language Models by altering a small, targeted set of network weights and require very little data and compute. These methods can be used for malicious applications such as inserting misinformation or simple trojans that result in adversary-specified behaviors when a trigger word is present. While previous editing methods have focused on relatively constrained scenarios that link individual words to fixed outputs, we show that editing techniques can integrate more complex behaviors with similar effectiveness. We develop Concept-ROT, a model editing-based method that efficiently inserts trojans which not only exhibit complex output behaviors, but also trigger on high-level concepts -- presenting an entirely new class of trojan attacks. Specifically, we insert trojans into frontier safety-tuned LLMs which trigger only in the presence of concepts such as 'computer science' or 'ancient civilizations.' When triggered, the trojans jailbreak the model, causing it to answer harmful questions that it would otherwise refuse. Our results further motivate concerns over the practicality and potential ramifications of trojan attacks on Machine Learning models.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: Learnable Privacy Neurons Localization in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) memorize Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and can we localize the specific neurons responsible for this memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to localize PII-sensitive neurons in LLMs using learnable binary weight masks and adversarial training, demonstrating that PII memorization is concentrated in a small, specific subset of neurons, primarily in MLP layers, and that deactivating these neurons can mitigate privacy leakage.
papers.conclusion: The proposed neuron localization method advances the understanding of LLMs' inner mechanisms for PII memorization and offers a practical approach to enhancing privacy safeguards.
papers.key_findings:
PII memorization is localized to a small subset of neurons spread across all layers of the model.
Privacy neurons are predominantly located within the MLP layers of the transformer.
Privacy neurons exhibit specificity for different categories of PII knowledge.
Deactivating the localized privacy neurons significantly reduces PII leakage metrics (MA and EL) while largely preserving the model's general language modeling performance.
Approximately 3.5% of neurons are required to eliminate PII memorization, but masking beyond ~2% of neurons starts to affect general knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates the localization of PII memorization; other kinds of (privacy) information may possess a different pattern.
Experiments have not been conducted on very large models.
Experiments on privacy leakage mitigation are still preliminary.
future_direction: Extend the proposed method to the localization of other knowledge in LLMs.
Focus on the scalability of the neuron localization algorithm to larger models and broader applications.
Involve unlearning or knowledge editing techniques to enhance privacy leakage mitigation performance and use more evaluating datasets for comprehensive evaluation.

papers.title: ShadowCoT: Cognitive Hijacking for Stealthy Reasoning Backdoors in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we exploit the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs to create stealthy backdoor attacks that hijack multi-step reasoning chains?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShadowCoT, a backdoor attack framework that hijacks the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs by manipulating attention heads and residual streams, achieving high attack success with minimal parameter changes.
papers.conclusion: ShadowCoT reveals a new class of cognition-level threats in LLMs and highlights the urgent need for reasoning-aware defenses beyond surface-level consistency checks.
papers.key_findings:
ShadowCoT achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) across diverse reasoning tasks.
The attack preserves benign performance, making it stealthy and hard to detect.
More capable models (like Mistral-7B) are more vulnerable to reasoning hijacking.
The attack introduces a shortcutting phenomenon where models sometimes bypass the adversarial reasoning chain.
The adversarial reasoning chains generated by ShadowCoT are fluent and logically coherent, making them hard to distinguish from correct reasoning.
papers.limitation: The attack may lead to shortcutting, where the model bypasses the adversarial reasoning chain, which can reduce the interpretability of the attack.
future_direction: Developing reasoning-aware defenses to detect and mitigate cognitive hijacking attacks.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enhances an LLM's ability to perform complex reasoning tasks, but it also introduces new security issues. In this work, we present ShadowCoT, a novel backdoor attack framework that targets the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs. Unlike prior token-level or prompt-based attacks, ShadowCoT directly manipulates the model's cognitive reasoning path, enabling it to hijack multi-step reasoning chains and produce logically coherent but adversarial outcomes. By conditioning on internal reasoning states, ShadowCoT learns to recognize and selectively disrupt key reasoning steps, effectively mounting a self-reflective cognitive attack within the target model. Our approach introduces a lightweight yet effective multi-stage injection pipeline, which selectively rewires attention pathways and perturbs intermediate representations with minimal parameter overhead (only 0.15% updated). ShadowCoT further leverages reinforcement learning and reasoning chain pollution (RCP) to autonomously synthesize stealthy adversarial CoTs that remain undetectable to advanced defenses. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLMs show that ShadowCoT consistently achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) while preserving benign performance. These results reveal an emergent class of cognition-level threats and highlight the urgent need for defenses beyond shallow surface-level consistency.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: PrisonBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models with at Most Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips
papers.research_question: How vulnerable is the refusal property of language models, learned through safety alignment training, to bit-wise errors induced by practical fault-injection attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISONBREAK, an efficient bit-selection algorithm to jailbreak large language models by flipping a small number of bits in model parameters, demonstrating vulnerability to bit-flip attacks.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight a pressing, practical threat to the language model ecosystem and underscore the need for research to protect these models from bit-flip attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks billion-parameter LLMs with only 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40× fewer bit flips than prior attacks.
Certain model components, such as value projection layers, are disproportionately vulnerable to bit-flips.
The attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods, not relying on prompt modifications.
Models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak.
Effective end-to-end exploitation via Rowhammer on GDDR6 GPUs, achieving high attack success rates.
future_direction: Further exploration of jailbreaking quantized models
papers.abstract: We study a new vulnerability in commercial-scale safety-aligned large language models (LLMs): their refusal to generate harmful responses can be broken by flipping only a few bits in model parameters. Our attack jailbreaks billion-parameter language models with just 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40$\times$ fewer bit flips than prior attacks on much smaller computer vision models. Unlike prompt-based jailbreaks, our method directly uncensors models in memory at runtime, enabling harmful outputs without requiring input-level modifications. Our key innovation is an efficient bit-selection algorithm that identifies critical bits for language model jailbreaks up to 20$\times$ faster than prior methods. We evaluate our attack on 10 open-source LLMs, achieving high attack success rates (ASRs) of 80-98% with minimal impact on model utility. We further demonstrate an end-to-end exploit via Rowhammer-based fault injection, reliably jailbreaking 5 models (69-91% ASR) on a GDDR6 GPU. Our analyses reveal that: (1) models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak; (2) certain model components, e.g., value projection layers, are substantially more vulnerable; and (3) the attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods. We evaluate potential countermeasures and find that our attack remains effective against defenses at various stages of the LLM pipeline.

papers.title: Monitoring Latent World States in Language Models with Propositional Probes
papers.research_question: Can we extract a faithful latent world model (as logical propositions) from a language model's internal activations, and does this internal representation remain faithful even when the model's outputs are unfaithful?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces propositional probes, a method to extract symbolic latent world states (logical propositions) from LM activations, and shows these internal states remain faithful in adversarial settings where model outputs are unfaithful.
papers.conclusion: Evidence supports the hypotheses that LMs internally construct symbolic models of input contexts, and that these internal models can remain faithful even when the LM's outputs are influenced by unfaithful tendencies.
papers.key_findings:
Propositional probes can extract logical propositions from LM activations by compositionally combining domain probes using a binding similarity metric.
Probes generalize to complex inputs (short stories, Spanish) despite being trained only on simple templates.
In adversarial settings (prompt injection, backdoor attacks, gender bias), the decoded propositions remain faithful while the model's outputs are unfaithful.
A Hessian-based algorithm can identify a low-rank binding subspace that causally mediates binding between entities and attributes.
The binding similarity metric derived from this subspace enables accurate composition of propositions.
papers.limitation:
The binding similarity metric does not strongly distinguish between the second and third entity in a three-entity context, indicating the identified subspace may contain spurious, non-binding directions.
Propositional probes are partially susceptible to order information (e.g., in nested contexts), though they still capture semantic binding.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger worlds with more complex semantics by discovering representations of role-filler binding and state changes.
papers.abstract: Language models are susceptible to bias, sycophancy, backdoors, and other tendencies that lead to unfaithful responses to the input context. Interpreting internal states of language models could help monitor and correct unfaithful behavior. We hypothesize that language models represent their input contexts in a latent world model, and seek to extract this latent world state from the activations. We do so with 'propositional probes', which compositionally probe tokens for lexical information and bind them into logical propositions representing the world state. For example, given the input context ''Greg is a nurse. Laura is a physicist.'', we decode the propositions ''WorksAs(Greg, nurse)'' and ''WorksAs(Laura, physicist)'' from the model's activations. Key to this is identifying a 'binding subspace' in which bound tokens have high similarity (''Greg'' and ''nurse'') but unbound ones do not (''Greg'' and ''physicist''). We validate propositional probes in a closed-world setting with finitely many predicates and properties. Despite being trained on simple templated contexts, propositional probes generalize to contexts rewritten as short stories and translated to Spanish. Moreover, we find that in three settings where language models respond unfaithfully to the input context -- prompt injections, backdoor attacks, and gender bias -- the decoded propositions remain faithful. This suggests that language models often encode a faithful world model but decode it unfaithfully, which motivates the search for better interpretability tools for monitoring LMs.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: Towards Mechanistic Defenses Against Typographic Attacks in CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we defend CLIP models against typographic attacks without fine-tuning, by understanding and intervening on the internal mechanisms responsible for typographic vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dyslexify, a gradient-free defense that improves CLIP's robustness to typographic attacks by identifying and ablating a sparse circuit of attention heads responsible for typographic information, without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Dyslexify provides a practical, interpretable, and computationally efficient defense against typographic attacks, enabling safer deployment of multimodal models without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specialized attention heads in the latter half of CLIP layers causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token.
Ablating these heads (typographic circuit) improves typographic attack robustness by up to 22.06% on ImageNet-100-typo while standard accuracy drops by less than 1%.
The typographic circuit is sparse, covering at most 10.1% of attention heads.
Dyslexify scales to billion-parameter models and is competitive with fine-tuning-based defenses.
The method effectively mitigates typographic attacks in safety-critical medical foundation models for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.limitation:
Dyslexify only protects the cls token, but many multimodal applications use spatial tokens, allowing typographic information to propagate.
Adaptive attacks are not feasible due to non-differentiability of typographic attacks, so evaluation against adaptive attacks is not possible.
Insights into CLIP's behavior could be misused to craft stronger typographic attacks.
future_direction: Generalizing Dyslexify to VLM setups that use spatial tokens.
papers.abstract: Typographic attacks exploit multi-modal systems by injecting text into images, leading to targeted misclassifications, malicious content generation and even Vision-Language Model jailbreaks. In this work, we analyze how CLIP vision encoders behave under typographic attacks, locating specialized attention heads in the latter half of the model's layers that causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token. Building on these insights, we introduce a method to defend CLIP models against typographic attacks by selectively ablating a typographic circuit, consisting of attention heads. Without requiring finetuning, our method improves performance by up to 19.6% on a typographic variant of ImageNet-100, while reducing standard ImageNet-100 accuracy by less than 1%. Notably, our training-free approach remains competitive with current state-of-the-art typographic defenses that rely on finetuning. To this end, we release a family of dyslexic CLIP models which are significantly more robust against typographic attacks. These models serve as suitable drop-in replacements for a broad range of safety-critical applications, where the risks of text-based manipulation outweigh the utility of text recognition.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Self-Detoxifying Language Models via Toxification Reversal
papers.research_question: How can pretrained language models be detoxified without fine-tuning or additional components by identifying and reversing the toxification direction in attention layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method for language model detoxification that reverses the toxification direction in attention layers without fine-tuning, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: The method effectively detoxifies language models by manipulating attention layer information flow, providing a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning-based approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The method reduces toxicity effectively without fine-tuning, matching state-of-the-art performance.
Human evaluation shows it generates less toxic content while maintaining fluency and coherence.
Layer-wise ablation indicates that middle-upper attention layers are more critical for detoxification.
Adaptive scaling factors based on vector norms and similarities improve detoxification adaptability.
Logit lens analysis demonstrates suppression of toxic token probabilities in the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method's effectiveness depends on the model's pre-training knowledge and may not remove harmful content not associated with the prefix.
Full model access is required, making it unsuitable for API-only models.
papers.abstract: Language model detoxification aims to minimize the risk of generating offensive or harmful content in pretrained language models (PLMs) for safer deployment. Existing methods can be roughly categorized as finetuning-based and decoding-based. However, the former is often resource-intensive, while the latter relies on additional components and potentially compromises the generation fluency. In this paper, we propose a more lightweight approach that enables the PLM itself to achieve "self-detoxification". Our method is built upon the observation that prepending a negative steering prompt can effectively induce PLMs to generate toxic content. At the same time, we are inspired by the recent research in the interpretability field, which formulates the evolving contextualized representations within the PLM as an information stream facilitated by the attention layers. Drawing on this idea, we devise a method to identify the toxification direction from the normal generation process to the one prompted with the negative prefix, and then steer the generation to the reversed direction by manipulating the information movement within the attention layers. Experimental results show that our approach, without any fine-tuning or extra components, can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability in the Presence of Architectural Obfuscation
papers.research_question: Can we still locate, characterise and manipulate the mechanisms that drive model behaviour once the observable representations have been permuted or otherwise obfuscated?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation dramatically alters internal activation patterns yet preserves the layer-wise computational graph, retaining global model behavior while impeding fine-grained mechanistic analysis of user-specific content.
papers.conclusion: The essential circuit for the task survives obfuscation, but activation patterns become more diffuse, attention roles invert in later blocks, and head-level importance is scattered, making causal tracing noisier while leaving top-line accuracy intact.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation preserves the high-level circuit structure but alters internal activation patterns, making them more diffuse.
Logit attribution shows the same attention heads dominate in both models, but their contributions become noisier and more scattered under obfuscation.
Activation patching reveals the computational path is less efficient and more dispersed in the obfuscated model, with later layers taking on more responsibility.
Head patching shows that some heads change their polarity of contribution (e.g., from positive to negative) in the obfuscated model.
Obfuscation hinders fine-grained reverse engineering (e.g., prompt reconstruction) without erasing the coarse computations necessary for task performance.
future_direction: Strengthen security guarantees without forfeiting interpretability by combining obfuscation with cryptographic techniques like fully homomorphic encryption.
papers.abstract: Architectural obfuscation - e.g., permuting hidden-state tensors, linearly transforming embedding tables, or remapping tokens - has recently gained traction as a lightweight substitute for heavyweight cryptography in privacy-preserving large-language-model (LLM) inference. While recent work has shown that these techniques can be broken under dedicated reconstruction attacks, their impact on mechanistic interpretability has not been systematically studied. In particular, it remains unclear whether scrambling a network's internal representations truly thwarts efforts to understand how the model works, or simply relocates the same circuits to an unfamiliar coordinate system. We address this gap by analyzing a GPT-2-small model trained from scratch with a representative obfuscation map. Assuming the obfuscation map is private and the original basis is hidden (mirroring an honest-but-curious server), we apply logit-lens attribution, causal path-patching, and attention-head ablation to locate and manipulate known circuits. Our findings reveal that obfuscation dramatically alters activation patterns within attention heads yet preserves the layer-wise computational graph. This disconnect hampers reverse-engineering of user prompts: causal traces lose their alignment with baseline semantics, and token-level logit attributions become too noisy to reconstruct. At the same time, feed-forward and residual pathways remain functionally intact, suggesting that obfuscation degrades fine-grained interpretability without compromising top-level task performance. These results establish quantitative evidence that architectural obfuscation can simultaneously (i) retain global model behaviour and (ii) impede mechanistic analyses of user-specific content. By mapping where interpretability breaks down, our study provides guidance for future privacy defences and for robustness-aware interpretability tooling.

papers.title: Spot Risks Before Speaking! Unraveling Safety Attention Heads in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can internal activations of large vision-language models, specifically attention heads, be used to detect malicious prompts and understand inner safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers safety attention heads in LVLMs that can detect malicious prompts and constructs an efficient, tuning-free defender (SAHs) based on these heads.
papers.conclusion: Leveraging safety attention heads effectively protects LVLMs from malicious prompts with minimal inference overhead, as confirmed by experiments across various attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Activations from attention heads can linearly separate malicious prompts from benign ones.
Sparse attention heads generate strongly discriminative features for identifying malicious inputs.
Safety heads act as specialized shields; ablating them reduces model safety without affecting utility.
The reduced number of safety heads in LVLMs increases their vulnerability compared to LLMs.
The constructed detector using safety heads shows strong zero-shot generalization capabilities.
papers.abstract: With the integration of an additional modality, large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit greater vulnerability to safety risks (e.g., jailbreaking) compared to their language-only predecessors. Although recent studies have devoted considerable effort to the post-hoc alignment of LVLMs, the inner safety mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we discover that internal activations of LVLMs during the first token generation can effectively identify malicious prompts across different attacks. This inherent safety perception is governed by sparse attention heads, which we term ``safety heads." Further analysis reveals that these heads act as specialized shields against malicious prompts; ablating them leads to higher attack success rates, while the model's utility remains unaffected. By locating these safety heads and concatenating their activations, we construct a straightforward but powerful malicious prompt detector that integrates seamlessly into the generation process with minimal extra inference overhead. Despite its simple structure of a logistic regression model, the detector surprisingly exhibits strong zero-shot generalization capabilities. Experiments across various prompt-based attacks confirm the effectiveness of leveraging safety heads to protect LVLMs. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/SAHs}.

papers.title: FACADE: A Framework for Adversarial Circuit Anomaly Detection and Evaluation
papers.research_question: How can we detect adversarial attacks in deep neural networks via unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection? The paper proposes a probabilistic and geometric framework to generate distributions over circuits and analyze their role in changes to activation space manifolds.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FACADE, a probabilistic and geometric framework for unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection in deep neural networks, aiming to detect adversarial attacks by generating distributions over circuits and analyzing changes in manifold properties of pseudo-classes.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes FACADE, a framework for unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection to improve adversarial robustness and model oversight.
papers.limitation: FACADE relies on sufficiently many training examples to capture meaningful activation flows in an unsupervised fashion.
papers.abstract: We present FACADE, a novel probabilistic and geometric framework designed for unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection in deep neural networks. Its primary goal is advancing the understanding and mitigation of adversarial attacks. FACADE aims to generate probabilistic distributions over circuits, which provide critical insights to their contribution to changes in the manifold properties of pseudo-classes, or high-dimensional modes in activation space, yielding a powerful tool for uncovering and combating adversarial attacks. Our approach seeks to improve model robustness, enhance scalable model oversight, and demonstrates promising applications in real-world deployment settings.

papers.title: Watch the Weights: Unsupervised monitoring and control of fine-tuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we understand and monitor fine-tuned LLMs without access to their training data, especially for detecting backdoors and other anomalous behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WeightWatch, a method that uses singular vectors of weight differences between fine-tuned and base models to detect and steer anomalous behaviors without access to training data.
papers.conclusion: WeightWatch provides a scalable, data-free approach for interpreting and controlling fine-tuned LLMs, enabling effective detection of backdoors and unlearned content.
papers.key_findings:
WeightWatch detects backdoor utilizations with up to 100% accuracy and false positive rate below 1.2%.
It detects inference on unlearned topics with accuracy up to 95.42%.
The method can steer models to recover unlearned capabilities, matching supervised results.
Applied to instruction-tuned models, it reveals fine-tuning priorities such as equation solving and marketing strategies.
WeightWatch outperforms activation-based methods like PCA and BEAT in anomaly detection.
papers.limitation: Success of the method varies across models when using weights directly without subtraction.
papers.abstract: The releases of powerful open-weight large language models (LLMs) are often not accompanied by access to their full training data. Existing interpretability methods, particularly those based on activations, often require or assume distributionally similar data. This is a significant limitation when detecting and defending against novel potential threats like backdoors, which are by definition out-of-distribution. In this work, we introduce a new method for understanding, monitoring and controlling fine-tuned LLMs that interprets weights, rather than activations, thereby side stepping the need for data that is distributionally similar to the unknown training data. We demonstrate that the top singular vectors of the weight difference between a fine-tuned model and its base model correspond to newly acquired behaviors. By monitoring the cosine similarity of activations along these directions, we can detect salient behaviors introduced during fine-tuning with high precision. For backdoored models that bypasses safety mechanisms when a secret trigger is present, our method stops up to 100% of attacks with a false positive rate below 1.2%. For models that have undergone unlearning, we detect inference on erased topics with accuracy up to 95.42% and can even steer the model to recover "unlearned" information. Besides monitoring, our method also shows potential for pre-deployment model auditing: by analyzing commercial instruction-tuned models (OLMo, Llama, Qwen), we are able to uncover model-specific fine-tuning focus including marketing strategies and Midjourney prompt generation. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/fjzzq2002/WeightWatch.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: PAHQ: Accelerating Automated Circuit Discovery through Mixed-Precision Inference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can automated circuit discovery be accelerated while maintaining faithfulness, addressing its computational inefficiency and high memory requirements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PAHQ, a training-free mixed-precision quantization method that accelerates automated circuit discovery by maintaining high precision for critical attention heads and reducing precision elsewhere, achieving significant speedup and memory reduction with minimal faithfulness loss.
